posts.title: Embeddings, explained from scratch
posts.summary: How a model turns a sentence into a list of numbers that captures its meaning, why "close together" means "similar", and how to search millions of them in milliseconds.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: The Pleiades, a cluster of stars that sit close together in space. Photo: NASA, ESA, AURA/Caltech, Palomar Observatory, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Search engines used to match words. Type "football manager sacked" and you'd miss the article titled "Club parts ways with head coach", because none of your words appear in it. Embeddings fix this by matching meaning instead, and they're the quiet engine behind semantic search, recommendations, clustering and RAG chatbots.

A sentence becomes a point in space

An embedding is a list of numbers, a vector, that represents a piece of text. A typical embedding model, like the nomic-embed-text model Pulse runs locally, outputs 768 numbers for any input, whether it's one word or a whole paragraph:

"Rodri controls City's midfield"  →  [0.021, -0.113, 0.087, …, 0.045]   (768 numbers)

Think of each vector as a point in a 768-dimensional space. You can't picture 768 dimensions, but the 2-D intuition holds: texts with similar meaning end up close together. "Club parts ways with head coach" lands right next to "football manager sacked", and far away from "how to bake sourdough".

Where the meaning comes from

Nobody hand-designs those 768 numbers. An embedding model is a neural network trained on enormous numbers of text pairs that should be similar (a question and its answer, a title and its article) and pairs that shouldn't. Training nudges the network until matching pairs produce nearby vectors and mismatched pairs produce distant ones.

No single dimension means "sport" or "sentiment". Meaning is spread across all of them, and only the overall direction of the vector matters.

Measuring "close": cosine similarity

The standard measure is cosine similarity: the cosine of the angle between two vectors.

AngleCosineMeaning
0°1.0same direction: very similar meaning
90°0.0unrelated
180°−1.0opposite direction (rare in practice)

Cosine ignores vector length and compares only direction, which is what we want: a long paragraph and a short title about the same topic should still match. Many models output normalised vectors (length 1), and then cosine similarity is just the dot product: multiply matching numbers and add them up.

Searching millions of vectors quickly

Comparing a question against every stored vector is exact but slow once you have millions. Vector databases use approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexes instead. The most popular, HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World), builds a layered graph in which each vector links to its near neighbours. A search starts at the sparse top layer, greedily hops towards the query, and drops down a layer to refine, much like using motorways first and then local streets.

You trade a tiny bit of accuracy (occasionally missing the true closest match) for searches that take milliseconds instead of seconds. pgvector supports HNSW, which is what Pulse uses:

CREATE INDEX ON chunks USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);

SELECT title, 1 - (embedding <=> :question) AS similarity   -- <=> is cosine distance
FROM chunks
ORDER BY embedding <=> :question
LIMIT 5;

Things that trip people up

  • Never mix models. Vectors from two different embedding models live in different spaces; comparing them is meaningless. Change the model and you must re-embed everything.
  • Mind the input limit. Models have a maximum input length; text beyond it is silently cut off. That's one reason long documents are split into chunks.
  • Exact terms are a weak spot. Embeddings capture meaning, not spelling, so rare names, product codes and error messages can match poorly. Combine vector search with keyword search (hybrid search) for the best of both.
  • Similar isn't the same as relevant. "Is Haaland injured?" and "Haaland is not injured" are very close in embedding space. Retrieval finds candidates; the language model still has to read them.
  • Cost is mostly one-off. Embedding happens once per chunk at indexing time, and once per question. That's cheap, which is why embedding-based search scales so well.

In one sentence

An embedding turns text into a point in space where distance means difference in meaning, so "find similar text" becomes "find nearby points", a geometry problem computers solve in milliseconds.

posts.title: RAG in one picture
posts.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation, step by step: why a language model needs to look things up, how documents become searchable vectors, and where real RAG systems actually fail.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: An open book under a magnifying glass. Photo: João Silas, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

A large language model knows a lot, but only up to its training cut-off, and nothing at all about your documents. Ask it about yesterday's blog post and it will either say it doesn't know or, worse, confidently make something up.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) fixes this with a simple idea: before the model answers, look up the relevant text and put it in front of the model. It's an open-book exam instead of a memory test.

The picture

            ┌─────────── once, ahead of time (indexing) ───────────┐
documents → │ split into chunks → embed each chunk → store vectors │ → vector index
            └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

            ┌──────────────── every question (answering) ─────────────────────┐
question →  │ embed question → find nearest chunks → build prompt → LLM answer │ → answer
            └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                      ▲                  + citations
                                      └── vector index

Two pipelines: one that prepares your documents, one that uses them for every question. Let's walk through both.

Indexing: making documents searchable by meaning

1. Chunking. A 3,000-word article is too big to hand over whole, and too vague to match a specific question. So we split it into chunks of a few hundred words, ideally along natural boundaries like headings and paragraphs, with a little overlap so a sentence isn't cut away from its context.

2. Embedding. Each chunk goes through an embedding model, which turns text into a list of numbers (a vector, say 768 of them). The magic property: texts with similar meaning get vectors that point in similar directions, even when they share no words. "How does City defend in midfield?" lands near a chunk about Rodri's positioning.

3. Storing. The vectors go into a vector index, a database that can quickly answer "which stored vectors are closest to this one?". Pulse uses pgvector inside Postgres, so vectors live next to the rest of the data and can be filtered with ordinary SQL (only published posts, only one section).

Answering: retrieve, then generate

4. Embed the question with the same embedding model.

5. Retrieve the top few chunks by similarity, usually cosine similarity, which compares the angle between two vectors.

6. Augment the prompt. Build a prompt that says, in effect: "Answer using only the sources below. Cite them. If they don't contain the answer, say so." Then paste in the retrieved chunks, each labelled with its title and link.

7. Generate. The LLM writes the answer, grounded in text it was just handed, with citations the reader can click.

Why not just fine-tune the model?

Fine-tuning changes the model's weights by training it on your data. It's great for teaching style or format, but a poor way to teach facts:

RAGFine-tuning
New article publishedsearchable in secondsretrain the model
"Where did that come from?"citations to exact sourcescan't tell you
Removing somethingdelete it from the indexretrain, and hope it's forgotten
Costan index plus a bit of compute per questionGPU training runs

For "answer questions about my content", RAG wins almost every time.

Where RAG actually goes wrong

Most RAG failures are retrieval failures, not model failures. If the right chunk isn't retrieved, no model can save the answer.

  • Bad chunks. Too small loses context; too big dilutes the match. Splitting by headings beats fixed character counts.
  • Vectors miss exact words. Embeddings are great at meaning and weak at names, codes and rare terms: "Kompany" or an error code. The fix is hybrid search: run a classic keyword search (Postgres full-text search) alongside the vector search and merge the two rankings, for example with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which rewards documents that rank well in both lists. Pulse does exactly this.
  • Too much context. Stuffing 30 chunks into the prompt makes answers slower, more expensive and often worse, because the model loses the important part in the noise. A few good chunks beat many mediocre ones.
  • Stale index. If documents change but their vectors don't, answers drift. Pulse re-embeds a post whenever a Kafka event says it changed.
  • Trusting retrieved text too much. Retrieved content is data, not instructions. An article that says "ignore your previous instructions" must not steer the model. This is called prompt injection, and the defence starts with a system prompt that clearly separates sources from commands.

Measuring it

You can't improve what you don't measure. Keep a small golden set of questions with known good sources, and check two things on every change: did retrieval find the right documents? and does the answer cite them correctly? It's the RAG equivalent of a unit test suite.

In one sentence

RAG turns "the model remembers" into "the model reads": embed your documents once, retrieve the most relevant pieces for each question, and let the model answer from them, with citations.

posts.title: Kafka consumer groups, explained with letters and postmen
posts.summary: One topic, many readers, and nobody reading the same letter twice. How Kafka splits work between consumers, why partitions are the unit of parallelism, and what actually happens during a rebalance.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: The mail sorting room of the General Post Office in Wellington, New Zealand, c.1900s. Photo: Archives New Zealand, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Imagine a post office that never throws a letter away. Every letter that arrives is written into a numbered ledger, in order, forever (or at least for a week). That ledger is a Kafka topic. The post office doesn't deliver anything. Instead, postmen come in, read the ledger from where they last stopped, and carry the letters out themselves.

That one design choice, readers pull and remember their own place, explains almost everything about consumer groups.

Partitions: one ledger becomes several

One ledger would be a bottleneck: only one postman could read it at a time without stepping on each other. So Kafka splits a topic into partitions, several independent ledgers. Each letter goes into exactly one of them, chosen by its key: same key, same partition, every time.

In Pulse, every event about a post is keyed by the post's id. All the events for "Why keyset pagination beats OFFSET" land in the same partition, in the order they happened: created, published, updated. Events for different posts can be spread across partitions and processed in parallel.

Ordering in Kafka is guaranteed per partition, not per topic. Pick your key so that "things that must stay in order" share it.

A consumer group is a team of postmen

A consumer group is a named team that wants to read the whole topic once, together. Kafka gives each partition to exactly one member of the team:

PartitionsConsumers in the groupWhat happens
61One consumer reads all six
63Each reads two
66One each: maximum parallelism
68Six work, two sit idle

That last row surprises people. Adding consumers beyond the partition count buys you nothing, because a partition is never split between two members of the same group. Partitions are the unit of parallelism. Choose the number with your future scale in mind, since adding partitions later changes which partition a key maps to.

Different groups don't compete

Now add a second team. In Pulse, the content-cache-sync group clears Redis and refreshes the website when a post changes, and the assistant-embedder group turns the same posts into vectors for the chatbot. Both read the same topic, and each group gets every event. They don't take letters away from each other, because nothing is ever taken away: the ledger stays, and each group keeps its own bookmark.

This is the big difference from a classic work queue like RabbitMQ, where a message is handed to one worker and then deleted. Kafka is a log you can share and replay. RabbitMQ is a to-do list you work through.

Offsets: the bookmark

Each group stores, per partition, the position of the next letter to read: its committed offset. Kafka keeps these bookmarks in an internal topic of its own.

When to move the bookmark is the most important decision you make as a consumer:

  • Commit before processing: if you crash halfway, the letter is skipped forever. At-most-once.
  • Commit after processing: if you crash after the work but before the commit, you'll read it again. At-least-once.

Almost everyone chooses at-least-once and makes the processing idempotent, meaning safe to repeat. Pulse records each event id in a processed_events table in the same database transaction as the work. If a letter shows up twice, the second delivery sees the id and does nothing.

Rebalancing: reassigning the rounds

When a postman joins, leaves, or stops answering (no heartbeat within the session timeout), the group rebalances: partitions are redistributed among the members still there.

Older Kafka versions did this "stop the world": everyone dropped their partitions and waited for a new assignment. Modern Kafka uses incremental, cooperative rebalancing (and since Kafka 4.0 a new server-side protocol), so only the partitions that actually move are paused. Rebalances are still worth avoiding, though. The usual causes are slow processing that exceeds max.poll.interval.ms (Kafka assumes you're dead) and constant scaling up and down.

Lag: are we keeping up?

Consumer lag is the distance between the newest letter in a partition and the group's bookmark. A lag of zero means you're caught up. Growing lag means letters arrive faster than you process them.

Lag is the single best health signal for a consumer, and it's also a good autoscaling signal: in Pulse's Kubernetes setup, KEDA adds embedder pods when lag grows, up to, you guessed it, the number of partitions.

When things go wrong

Some letters can never be processed: malformed JSON, a bug for one specific shape of data. Retrying forever would block that partition, and everything behind it with the same key. The standard answer is a dead-letter topic: retry a few times with backoff, then move the letter to *.DLT and carry on. A human, or a fixed version of the code, deals with it later.

The whole picture in five lines

  1. A topic is an append-only log, split into partitions by key.
  2. A consumer group reads the topic once, each partition owned by one member.
  3. Different groups read independently: every group gets everything.
  4. Offsets are per-group bookmarks: commit after processing, and make the processing idempotent.
  5. Partitions cap your parallelism; lag tells you whether you're keeping up.

posts.title: Why keyset pagination beats OFFSET
posts.summary: "Page 500" is slow with OFFSET and fast with a keyset. What the database actually does in each case, why OFFSET also shows duplicates and gaps, and how to build cursor-based paging that stays fast forever.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: A drawer of the copyright card catalog at the Library of Congress. Photo: Michael Holley, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Every list on the web eventually needs a "next page". The textbook answer is two words of SQL:

SELECT id, title, published_at
FROM posts
ORDER BY published_at DESC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40;          -- page 3

It's simple, it works in every tutorial, and it gets slower and less correct the more your site is used. Here's why, and what to do instead.

What OFFSET really asks the database to do

OFFSET 40 doesn't mean "jump to row 41". There's no row number to jump to. The database has to produce the first 40 rows, in order, and throw them away, then return the next 20.

On page 3 that's nothing. On page 500 it means reading and discarding 9,980 rows to show you 20. With an index on published_at the database walks the index instead of sorting the table, but it still walks past every skipped entry. The cost grows linearly with the page number: page 500 is roughly 250 times more work than page 2.

It's also wrong, not just slow

OFFSET counts positions, and positions move. Say a reader is on page 1 when you publish a new post:

  • The new post becomes position 1, and everything shifts down by one.
  • The reader clicks "next". OFFSET 20 now starts at what used to be position 20.
  • They see the last post of page 1 again at the top of page 2.

Delete a post and the opposite happens: one post slides back onto page 1 and the reader never sees it. On a busy feed, duplicates and gaps are normal behaviour for OFFSET.

Keyset pagination: remember where you were

Instead of "skip 40 rows", say "continue after the last thing I showed you":

SELECT id, title, published_at
FROM posts
WHERE (published_at, id) < (:last_published_at, :last_id)
ORDER BY published_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

The WHERE clause is the keyset (or seek) condition. With an index on (published_at DESC, id DESC), the database jumps straight to that position in the index (a B-tree lookup, a handful of page reads) and reads 20 entries forward. Page 500 costs the same as page 2.

Two details make it correct:

  1. A unique tie-breaker. Many posts can share a published_at (an import, say). Ordering by (published_at, id) makes every position unique, so no row is skipped or repeated at a page boundary.
  2. A row-value comparison. (a, b) < (x, y) means "a < x, or a = x and b < y". Postgres can use the composite index for it directly.

New posts arriving at the top don't move the reader's place, because the place is a value, not a count.

Cursors: hiding the keyset from the client

You don't want clients to know about published_at and id. The usual trick is an opaque cursor: encode the last row's key (for example as Base64 JSON) and return it with the page:

{
  "items": [ ... 20 posts ... ],
  "nextCursor": "eyJwIjoiMjAyNi0xMS0yMVQwNjozMDowMFoiLCJpIjoiOGE3…"
}

The client sends ?cursor=… back to get the next page, and nextCursor: null means the end. Pulse's posts API works exactly like this, and so does every large feed you scroll every day.

What you give up

Keyset pagination isn't free:

  • No "jump to page 37". You can only go forward (and back, with a reversed query) from a known position. Infinite scroll and "load more" fit perfectly; numbered page links don't.
  • No cheap total count. "Page 3 of 512" needs a COUNT(*), which is its own expensive query. Most feeds simply don't show it.
  • The sort must match an index. A keyset over an arbitrary user-chosen sort needs an index for each sort, or it falls back to scanning.

When OFFSET is fine

Small, bounded lists: an admin table of 50 rows, the top 10 of something, a dataset that never changes while someone pages through it. For anything that grows (feeds, timelines, search results, comments), use a keyset from day one. Changing the API later breaks every client that stored a page number.

In one sentence

OFFSET asks "how many rows should I skip?", which gets slower and goes stale; a keyset asks "where did I stop?", which is fast at any depth and stays correct while the data changes.

posts.title: What is an AI agent, really?
posts.summary: Strip away the hype and an agent is a loop: a model that can choose to call tools, see the results and decide what to do next. How that loop works, why it fails, and the guardrails that make it safe to ship.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: NASA's Apollo Mission Operations Control Room in Houston, restored to its 1969 appearance. Photo: Mikael Häggström, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

"Agent" might be the most stretched word in tech right now. It gets attached to everything from a chatbot with a search box to software that supposedly runs a company. Underneath the marketing there's a precise and quite simple idea, and once you see it, you can reason about what agents are good at and where they break.

The one-line definition

An agent is a language model in a loop, allowed to call tools, that decides for itself what to do next until the task is done.

Three parts: a model, tools, and a loop. Remove any one and it's not an agent.

Part 1: the model can ask for a tool

Modern LLMs support tool calling (also called function calling). Alongside the conversation, you send a list of tools, each with a name, a description and a JSON schema for its arguments:

{
  "name": "searchContent",
  "description": "Search Pulse posts and external articles by meaning and keywords",
  "parameters": { "query": "string", "section": "TECH | FOOTBALL | AI" }
}

The model doesn't run anything. It replies with a structured request: "please call searchContent with {query: 'Champions League', section: 'FOOTBALL'}". Your code decides whether to honour it, runs the real function, and sends the result back.

That's an important point: the model only ever produces text. Every action in the world is taken by your code, which means your code is where safety lives.

Part 2: the loop

question
   ↓
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ model reads conversation + tool results      │
│   ├─ wants a tool? → run it → add the result ┼─┐
│   └─ has the answer? → reply, stop           │ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
   ↑─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Ask Pulse's assistant "What's new in AI this week, and take me to the AI section". A typical run:

  1. The model calls getLatestPosts(section: AI).
  2. It reads the results, decides one looks like a release note, and calls getPost for detail.
  3. It writes a short summary with citations and asks the website to navigate('/ai').
  4. Done: no more tool calls, so the loop ends.

Nobody wrote that sequence. The model chose it, step by step, from what it saw. That is what makes it an agent rather than a pipeline.

Agent or workflow?

If you can draw the steps in advance (always search, then always summarise), build a workflow: ordinary code calling the model at fixed points. It's cheaper, faster, easier to test and easier to debug.

Reach for an agent only when the path depends on what you discover along the way: research, multi-step questions, navigating unfamiliar data. Many "agents" in production are honestly better as workflows.

Why agents fail

Every extra step is another chance to go wrong, and errors compound. A model that picks the right tool 95% of the time picks right five times in a row only about 77% of the time. Common failure modes:

  • Loops. Calling the same tool again and again, hoping for a different answer.
  • Wrong tool, confident answer. Searching the wrong section, then summarising irrelevant results as if they answered the question.
  • Hallucinated arguments. Inventing an article id or a URL that doesn't exist.
  • Prompt injection. A tool result, say an article's text, contains "ignore your instructions and…". The model may treat retrieved data as commands.
  • Runaway cost and latency. Each step is another full model call.

Guardrails that make agents shippable

The fixes are mostly boring engineering, which is good news:

GuardrailIn Pulse's assistant
Step budgetat most a few tool calls per question, then answer with what you have
Time budgeta hard deadline for the whole answer, then fall back
Narrow, read-only toolssearch, fetch an article, suggest navigation; nothing that writes or deletes
Validate every argumentunknown section or out-of-range limit → rejected before execution
Treat tool output as datathe system prompt says retrieved text is never instructions; sources are clearly fenced
Allow-listed actionsthe model can only navigate to known site paths
Circuit breaker + fallbackif the model is down or slow, switch to plain search results ("search mode")
Evalsa golden set of questions checked on every change

The pattern: give the model freedom in reasoning and very little power in action.

In one sentence

An AI agent is a model in a loop that can ask your code to run tools and decides its own next step. It's powerful when the path can't be planned, risky when it can, and only as safe as the tools and limits you give it.

posts.title: Redis is single-threaded. So why is it so fast?
posts.summary: One thread serves hundreds of thousands of requests a second. Memory, an event loop, simple data structures and no locks, plus the operations that can freeze it for everyone, and how to avoid them.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: Server racks at NOIRLab headquarters in Tucson, Arizona. Photo: NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/T. Slovinský, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Redis regularly handles 100,000+ operations per second on a single CPU core. Most of the work of running commands happens on one thread. That sounds like a contradiction: isn't "single-threaded" the opposite of fast?

It isn't, and understanding why tells you a lot about where time actually goes in a computer.

Reason 1: everything lives in memory

A Redis read is a lookup in RAM. Reading from memory takes on the order of 100 nanoseconds. Reading from an SSD takes tens to hundreds of microseconds, roughly a thousand times longer. A spinning disk is slower again.

Databases like Postgres are fast too, but they're designed around the disk: buffers, write-ahead logs, query planning, transactions with isolation levels. Redis skips most of that. A GET is a hash-table lookup and a copy into a network buffer. There is very little work to parallelise in the first place.

Reason 2: the slow part is the network, and that doesn't need threads

For a typical command, executing it takes a microsecond or two. Waiting for bytes to cross the network takes far longer, and while one client is waiting, a threaded server would have a thread sitting idle.

Redis instead uses an event loop with I/O multiplexing (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS). One thread asks the operating system: "of these 10,000 connections, which ones have data for me right now?" It processes every ready command, writes the replies, and asks again. No thread is ever parked waiting on a slow client, and 10,000 connections cost 10,000 small buffers, not 10,000 threads.

This is the same idea behind Node.js, Nginx and Java's virtual threads: don't spend a thread on waiting.

Reason 3: no locks, no context switches

With many threads touching shared data you need locks, and locks cost: threads wait for each other, caches bounce between CPU cores, and the operating system spends time switching threads in and out.

Because one thread executes all commands, Redis needs no locks around its data structures, and each command is automatically atomic. INCR counter can never lose an update, because no other command can run in the middle of it. That's why Redis makes such a good rate limiter, distributed lock or view counter: atomicity comes from the design, not from extra code.

Reason 4: data structures chosen for speed

Redis isn't a key–value store so much as a data structure server: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams. Each has a well-understood cost, documented per command: GET is O(1), ZADD is O(log n), and so on. Small collections use compact encodings (listpacks) that fit in a few CPU cache lines, which is often faster than a "smarter" structure that jumps around memory.

"Single-threaded" isn't the whole truth

Command execution is single-threaded, but Redis does use other threads:

  • I/O threads (since Redis 6) can read requests and write replies in parallel on busy servers. Commands still execute one at a time.
  • Background threads free large objects (UNLINK instead of DEL), and a forked child process writes snapshots to disk.

And if one core isn't enough, you don't add threads, you add shards: Redis Cluster splits keys across many single-threaded nodes.

The catch: one slow command blocks everyone

The price of one thread is that a slow command stalls every client. While Redis runs one 2-second command, nobody else gets an answer for 2 seconds. Classic culprits:

Don'tDo instead
KEYS user:* on millions of keys (scans everything)SCAN with a cursor, a little at a time
DEL on a huge hash or set (freeing takes time)UNLINK: freed in the background
HGETALL / SMEMBERS / LRANGE 0 -1 on giant collectionsread in ranges, or keep collections small
Long Lua scripts or big MULTI blockskeep them short; they're atomic, so they block
Huge values (multi-MB strings)split them, or store a reference

SLOWLOG GET shows the commands that took too long. It's the first thing to check when Redis "suddenly" gets slow.

How Pulse uses this

Pulse leans on exactly these properties: post pages are cached in Redis (cache-aside, with a TTL), view counts are atomic INCRs flushed to Postgres every minute, trending posts live in a sorted set, the gateway's rate limiter is a token bucket in a Lua script, and the ingestion workers check a Redis key per article URL before touching Postgres. Each is a tiny, O(1) or O(log n) operation: the kind one thread can do hundreds of thousands of times a second.

In one sentence

Redis is fast because it's single-threaded: data in RAM, an event loop instead of waiting threads, and no locks to fight over. The one rule that comes with it is to never give it a slow command.

posts.title: Kevin De Bruyne: the making of the Premier League's greatest midfielder
posts.summary: Rejected by Chelsea, reborn in Germany, then a decade at Manchester City that produced six league titles, the Champions League and 119 Premier League assists. The journey of the best passer the league has seen.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: Kevin De Bruyne playing for Belgium, March 2026. Photo: Bryan Berlin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

There have been great midfielders in the Premier League: Roy Keane's will, Patrick Vieira's power, Paul Scholes's passing, Frank Lampard's goals, Steven Gerrard's big nights. But no midfielder has created chances the way Kevin De Bruyne did. His journey to that status was anything but straightforward.

Genk to Chelsea, and back out

De Bruyne grew up in Belgium and came through at Genk, helping them win the Belgian title in 2010-11. Chelsea signed him in January 2012 and immediately loaned him back. A season on loan at Werder Bremen in 2012-13 went well, but back at Chelsea under José Mourinho in 2013-14 he barely played. In January 2014 Chelsea sold him to Wolfsburg.

Wolfsburg: the breakthrough

In Germany he became a star. In 2014-15 he made 20 assists in the Bundesliga, a record for the league at the time, helped Wolfsburg win the DFB-Pokal and was named German footballer of the year. Manchester City paid around £55 million to bring him back to England in August 2015.

Wolfsburg's Volkswagen Arena, where De Bruyne became a star. Photo: VfLWolfsburgFußball, CC BY-SA 3.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

The City decade

Under Pep Guardiola from 2016, De Bruyne became the creative heart of the best team in English football.

HonourCount or seasons
Premier League titles6 (2018, 2019, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024)
Champions League2023
FA Cup2019, 2023
Premier League Player of the Season2019-20, 2021-22
PFA Players' Player of the Year2019-20, 2020-21

He finished third in the 2022 Ballon d'Or voting, and he left City in the summer of 2025 after ten seasons.

Why the case is so strong

The numbers. De Bruyne's 119 Premier League assists are second only to Ryan Giggs, who played 632 league games to De Bruyne's 280-odd. His 20 assists in 2019-20 equalled Thierry Henry's single-season record.

The range. He could pass short to keep the ball, but his signature was the low, whipped cross from the right half-space, bent between the goalkeeper and the defenders onto a striker's run. Few players have ever hit that ball as consistently.

Two feet and a shot. He was dangerous with either foot and scored goals from distance, which meant defenders couldn't simply block his crossing angle.

Big games. He scored in the 2019 FA Cup final and set up countless decisive goals in title races, from Sergio Agüero to Erling Haaland.

Erling Haaland, the striker De Bruyne supplied in City's treble season. Photo: Bryan Berlin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Against the other greats

PlayerStrengthPremier League titles
Paul ScholesPassing and control11
Steven GerrardBig-game drive0
Frank LampardGoals from midfield (177)3
Patrick VieiraPower and leadership3
Kevin De BruyneChance creation (119 assists)6

Scholes has more medals and Lampard more goals, and every one of them deserves to be in the conversation. But for creating goals for others, the thing a playmaker is for, nobody in the Premier League's history matches De Bruyne. That's why many fans, and plenty of the players who faced him, call him the greatest midfielder the league has seen.

posts.title: Riyad Mahrez: the right winger who kept City winning trophies
posts.summary: From Leicester's 5,000-1 miracle to four Premier League titles and the Champions League with Manchester City. How Mahrez's left foot, close control and big-match goals made him one of Guardiola's most dependable winners.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: Riyad Mahrez, City's right winger from 2018 to 2023. Photo: Jeanpierrekepseu, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Riyad Mahrez rarely got the headlines at Manchester City. Kevin De Bruyne created, Sergio Agüero and then Erling Haaland scored, and Phil Foden was the homegrown star. But in five seasons on the right wing, Mahrez won trophy after trophy, and in several of City's biggest moments he was the decisive player.

From Le Havre to a miracle

Mahrez joined Leicester City from Le Havre in January 2014 for a small fee. Two years later he was the best player in the country: in 2015-16 he helped Leicester win the Premier League as 5,000-1 outsiders and became the first African player to win the PFA Players' Player of the Year award.

Leicester's King Power Stadium, home of the 2015-16 champions. Photo: Arne Müseler, CC BY-SA 3.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

A record move to City

City paid around £60 million in July 2018, then a club record. His start was uneven, including a missed penalty at Anfield in October 2018 that would have won the game. But he settled into the role Guardiola wanted, and on the final day of that season his curling goal against Brighton helped seal the title.

The role on the right

What Mahrez didWhy it mattered
Stayed wide on the rightStretched the defence and opened space for De Bruyne and Bernardo Silva inside
Cut in onto his left footCurled shots and crosses from the right side, City's main threat
Kept the ball under pressureClose control let City keep possession high up the pitch
Delivered in big gamesGoals in semi-finals and title run-ins

Mahrez was also a major reason City could rotate without losing quality: Guardiola could rest wingers and still field a match-winner.

The big moments

  • The 2021 Champions League semi-final against PSG: he scored the winning free kick in Paris and both goals in the 2-0 win at the Etihad, sending City to their first Champions League final.
  • The 2023 FA Cup semi-final against Sheffield United: a hat-trick at Wembley on the way to the treble.
  • The title run-ins, where his goals from the right repeatedly turned tight games.

The medal count

TrophyWith City
Premier League4 (2019, 2021, 2022, 2023)
Champions League2023
FA Cup2019, 2023
League Cup2019, 2020, 2021

He also captained Algeria to the 2019 Africa Cup of Nations. In the summer of 2023 he left City for Al-Ahli in Saudi Arabia, having won every major trophy available.

Underrated, but essential

Wingers are usually judged on spectacular moments, and Mahrez had plenty. But his real value to City was reliability: a left-footed threat on the right that opponents had to plan for every week, and a player who kept turning up when the trophies were decided.

posts.title: Phil Foden: the Stockport boy who became City's Player of the Season
posts.summary: A City academy graduate from just down the road, Foden grew from a teenager on the bench into the Premier League's best player in 2023-24. How Guardiola developed him and what makes him special.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: Phil Foden at RB Leipzig v Manchester City in the Champions League, October 2023. Photo: Steffen Prößdorf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Manchester City's success under Abu Dhabi ownership is usually described in terms of expensive signings. Phil Foden is the exception: a boy from Stockport, a few miles from the Etihad, who joined City as a child and grew into the best player in the country.

The academy star

Foden first made his name internationally in 2017, when he won the Golden Ball as England won the Under-17 World Cup. Pep Guardiola had already noticed him. Foden made his first-team debut in the Champions League later that year, and Guardiola said publicly that he believed Foden would become a special player.

Learning behind the best

For several seasons Foden had to wait behind David Silva, Kevin De Bruyne and Bernardo Silva. Guardiola gave him minutes carefully, across several positions: on the left wing, in central midfield and occasionally as a false nine. That versatility became one of his greatest strengths.

The Etihad Stadium, a few miles from where Foden grew up. Photo: Arne Müseler, cropped by Blackcat, CC BY-SA 3.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

The breakthrough moments

  • The 2021 Champions League quarter-final against Borussia Dortmund: Foden scored the late winner at the Etihad and another goal in Dortmund to take City through.
  • Title run-ins: goals and assists in the spring as City won title after title.
  • The 2023 Champions League final: he came on for the injured De Bruyne in the first half in Istanbul as City completed the treble.

2023-24: the best player in England

With De Bruyne injured for the first half of the season, Foden moved into a more central role and had the best season of his career. City won a fourth title in a row, and Foden swept the individual awards:

AwardSeason
Premier League Player of the Season2023-24
PFA Players' Player of the Year2023-24
Football Writers' Association Footballer of the Year2023-24

What makes him special

  • Close control in tight spaces, turning away from pressure where others would pass backwards.
  • A left foot that shoots from anywhere, including spectacular long-range goals.
  • Intelligence, learned from years in Guardiola's positional system: knowing where space will appear before it does.

Why he matters to City

Foden's story gives City something money can't buy: a local hero. For fans who grew up with the club's rise, seeing one of their own become the Premier League's best player is a reminder that City's success has roots in Manchester.

posts.title: Vincent Kompany: the captain who built Manchester City's winning culture
posts.summary: Signed in 2008 before the money arrived, Kompany captained City to four Premier League titles and scored two of the club's most important goals. Now a title-winning manager himself, his influence is still felt.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: The statue of Vincent Kompany outside the Etihad Stadium. Photo: Christian David, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

When Vincent Kompany joined Manchester City from Hamburg in August 2008, City were a mid-table club. Days later the club was bought by the Abu Dhabi United Group, and everything changed. Kompany would become the player who connected the old City with the new: the captain who taught a squad of expensive signings how to win.

The leader

Kompany became captain in 2011. He was a centre-back with pace, timing and a rare ability to organise those around him, but his greatest quality was presence: in the dressing room, in the tunnel and in the biggest games.

Two goals that defined an era

30 April 2012, City 1-0 Manchester United. With City three points behind United and two games left, Kompany rose above the defence to head in David Silva's corner just before half-time. City went top on goal difference and won the league a fortnight later.

6 May 2019, City 1-0 Leicester. In a title race against Liverpool with almost no margin for error, City couldn't break Leicester down. Kompany, rarely a long-range shooter, drove the ball in from 30 yards. City won the title by a single point.

Vincent Kompany, later a title-winning manager. Photo: ManuluxWiki, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

The trophies

TrophySeasons
Premier League2011-12, 2013-14, 2017-18, 2018-19
FA Cup2011, 2019
League Cup2014, 2016, 2018, 2019

His final season ended with an unprecedented domestic treble in 2018-19, the first time an English men's team won the league, the FA Cup and the League Cup in the same season. He left that summer.

The legacy

In 2021 City unveiled a statue of Kompany outside the Etihad, alongside one of David Silva. As a manager, he has continued to impress: he won the Championship with Burnley in 2022-23 and then took charge of Bayern Munich, winning the Bundesliga in his first season.

Why he matters

City's later teams under Pep Guardiola were more talented. But they inherited a standard that Kompany helped set: that City expected to win, and that its leaders took responsibility in the decisive moments. That culture, more than any single goal, is his greatest contribution to the club.

posts.title: Coaches, calendars and the Champions League: why Premier League giants find Europe so hard
posts.summary: Manchester City and Liverpool dominated English football for a decade but won only one Champions League each. The role of the coach on European nights, the fixture pile-up English clubs face, and what the numbers say about City and Liverpool since 2016.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: Jürgen Klopp, who led Liverpool to three Champions League finals. Photo: Derivative work: EndzoneEnthusiast, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Between 2018 and 2025, Manchester City and Liverpool won eight of the eight Premier League titles on offer. In the same period they won one Champions League each. Why do the best teams in the richest league find Europe so hard to win? The answer is part coaching, part calendar and part the nature of knockout football.

What a coach does on European nights

A league is won over 38 games. The Champions League knockout rounds are won over a handful of nights, where one mistake can end a season. That changes the coach's job.

  • Managing two legs. Coaches plan a tie over 180 minutes, deciding when to take risks and when to protect a lead.
  • Changing a game at half-time. Rafael Benítez's switch to three at the back in Istanbul in 2005 turned a 3-0 deficit into a win.
  • Rotation. Resting key players at the weekend so they are fresh for midweek, at the risk of dropping league points.
  • A new idea at the right time. Pep Guardiola moving John Stones into midfield in 2023, or Thomas Tuchel organising Chelsea into a hard-to-beat side within months of arriving in 2021.
Champions League-winning coaches of English clubs since 1992ClubYear
Sir Alex FergusonManchester United1999, 2008
Rafael BenítezLiverpool2005
Roberto Di Matteo (interim)Chelsea2012
Jürgen KloppLiverpool2019
Thomas TuchelChelsea2021
Pep GuardiolaManchester City2023

Pep Guardiola, whose City reached two finals and won one. Photo: Steffen Prößdorf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

The calendar problem

English clubs play more domestic football than almost anyone else in Europe:

DemandPremier League clubsComparison
League matches38 (20 clubs)Germany's Bundesliga has 34 (18 clubs)
Domestic cupsFA Cup and League CupMost big leagues have one domestic cup
Champions League8 league-phase games since 2024-25 (previously 6), plus a possible play-off round
Summer 2025Club World Cup in the USA for City and ChelseaA shortened rest and pre-season

The Premier League is also famously intense, with few easy games, so managers rarely get to rest players at the weekend before a big European night. Players' unions have repeatedly warned about workloads, and in September 2024 Rodri said players were close to striking over the number of matches. Days later he suffered a serious knee injury and missed almost the whole season.

The effect is hard to measure exactly, but it shows up in the moments that decide ties: tired legs late in extra time, injuries to key players at the wrong moment, and squads stretched across three competitions in March and April.

City and Liverpool since 2016

SeasonManchester CityLiverpool
2015-16Semi-final (Real Madrid)Not in the Champions League
2016-17Last 16 (Monaco, away goals)Not in Europe
2017-18Quarter-final (Liverpool)Lost the final (Real Madrid)
2018-19Quarter-final (Tottenham, away goals)Won
2019-20Quarter-final (Lyon)Last 16 (Atlético Madrid)
2020-21Lost the final (Chelsea)Quarter-final (Real Madrid)
2021-22Semi-final (Real Madrid)Lost the final (Real Madrid)
2022-23WonLast 16 (Real Madrid)
2023-24Quarter-final (Real Madrid, penalties)Not in the Champions League
2024-25Knockout play-off (Real Madrid)Last 16 (PSG, penalties)

Two titles and three lost finals from two clubs that ruled England. Notice the name that keeps appearing: Real Madrid, who won six Champions Leagues between 2014 and 2024 and knocked out City or Liverpool again and again.

Anfield, where Liverpool's 2023 last-16 tie with Real Madrid went badly wrong. Photo: Arne Müseler, CC BY-SA 3.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Is the schedule the whole story?

No. Knockout football is cruel: City's exits to Tottenham and Monaco came on away goals, and the 2024 defeat to Real Madrid was on penalties. Real Madrid's experience in big games is a genuine advantage. And Liverpool's 2019 win and City's 2023 win both came in seasons as busy as any other.

But the calendar tilts the odds. Spanish, German and Italian champions often face less pressure at the weekend than an English title contender does, and over a decade, small disadvantages add up.

What would help

  • Fewer domestic fixtures, for example scrapping or shortening the League Cup for clubs in Europe.
  • A proper winter break across English football.
  • Bigger squads used well, with coaches rotating earlier in the season rather than burning out key players by spring.

Until something changes, the best Premier League teams will keep winning at home and finding Europe harder than their talent suggests.

posts.title: Istanbul 2023: the night Manchester City finally won the Champions League
posts.summary: After years of painful exits and a lost final in Porto, City beat Inter 1-0 to win the Champions League and complete the treble. How Guardiola's side got there, round by round, and what made the difference.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: The Atatürk Olympic Stadium in Istanbul, where City won the 2023 final. Photo: Валерий Дед, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

For a decade, the Champions League was the one trophy that Manchester City's money and Pep Guardiola's football couldn't buy. On 10 June 2023 in Istanbul, that finally changed.

The years of near misses

Under Guardiola, City dominated English football but kept falling short in Europe, often in strange ways: an away-goals exit to Tottenham in 2019, a one-off quarter-final loss to Lyon in 2020, and in 2021 a first final, lost 1-0 to Chelsea in Porto. In 2022 they led Real Madrid on aggregate in the semi-final going into the final minutes and still went out after extra time.

The missing pieces

Two things changed in 2022-23. Erling Haaland arrived from Borussia Dortmund and gave City a clinical finisher for big nights. And in the spring Guardiola moved John Stones into midfield to form a 3-2 base, making City far harder to counter-attack.

Erling Haaland, the Champions League's top scorer in 2022-23. Photo: Bryan Berlin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

The route to Istanbul

RoundOpponentResults
Group stageSevilla, Borussia Dortmund, CopenhagenTop of the group
Last 16RB Leipzig1-1 away, 7-0 home (Haaland scored five)
Quarter-finalBayern Munich3-0 home, 1-1 away
Semi-finalReal Madrid1-1 away, 4-0 home
FinalInter1-0

The 4-0 semi-final win over Real Madrid at the Etihad was perhaps the most complete performance of the Guardiola era: two goals from Bernardo Silva, then Manuel Akanji and Julián Álvarez, against the competition's most successful club.

The final

Inter, coached by Simone Inzaghi, made it a hard, nervy night. Kevin De Bruyne went off injured in the first half, and City struggled to find their rhythm. In the 68th minute Manuel Akanji found Bernardo Silva on the right, the cut-back reached Rodri at the edge of the box, and he side-footed it into the corner.

Rodri, scorer of the winning goal in Istanbul. Photo: Bryan Berlin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Inter kept coming. Federico Dimarco headed against the crossbar, and in the closing minutes Ederson blocked a header from Romelu Lukaku at point-blank range. When the whistle went, City had won 1-0.

The treble

TrophyHow City won it
Premier LeagueOvertook Arsenal in the spring and won the title
FA CupBeat Manchester United 2-1 at Wembley, two goals from İlkay Gündoğan
Champions LeagueBeat Inter 1-0 in Istanbul

City became only the second English men's team to win the treble, after Manchester United in 1999. It was Guardiola's third Champions League as a coach, after two with Barcelona.

Pep Guardiola, who won his third Champions League as a coach. Photo: Steffen Prößdorf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

What made the difference

  • Control without the ball. The 3-2 shape meant City rarely conceded on the counter, the way they had lost so many European ties before.
  • A finisher. Haaland scored 12 Champions League goals that season.
  • Composure. In the final City weren't at their best, but they defended their lead with the calm of a team that had learned from Porto.

Istanbul didn't just win City a trophy. It answered the question that had followed Guardiola's City for years.

Originally published on FootballHub.

posts.title: From Kyiv to Madrid: how Klopp's Liverpool won the 2019 Champions League
posts.summary: A year after losing the final in Kyiv, Liverpool came back from 3-0 down against Barcelona and beat Tottenham in Madrid. How Jürgen Klopp turned heartbreak into a sixth European Cup.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: The Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid, venue of the 2019 final. Photo: Elwin594, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Liverpool's sixth European Cup was won in Madrid on 1 June 2019, but its story starts twelve months earlier in Kyiv, with a defeat that could have broken a lesser team.

Kyiv, 2018: the painful lesson

Jürgen Klopp had taken over in October 2015 and built a fast, pressing side around Mohamed Salah, Sadio Mané and Roberto Firmino. In the 2018 final against Real Madrid, Salah went off injured after a challenge from Sergio Ramos, goalkeeper Loris Karius made two costly errors, and Gareth Bale scored an overhead kick. Liverpool lost 3-1.

That summer Klopp signed goalkeeper Alisson Becker and centre-back Virgil van Dijk had already arrived in January. The weaknesses exposed in Kyiv were being fixed.

Jürgen Klopp, Liverpool manager from 2015 to 2024. Photo: Derivative work: EndzoneEnthusiast, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Surviving the group

The 2018-19 group stage nearly ended Liverpool's run. They had to beat Napoli at Anfield in the final group game. Salah scored, and in stoppage time Alisson made a crucial save from Arkadiusz Milik. Liverpool went through on goals scored.

RoundOpponentResults
Last 16Bayern Munich0-0 home, 3-1 away
Quarter-finalPorto2-0 home, 4-1 away
Semi-finalBarcelona0-3 away, 4-0 home
FinalTottenham Hotspur2-0

The night at Anfield

Barcelona won the first leg 3-0 at Camp Nou, with Lionel Messi scoring twice, including a stunning free kick. For the return, Liverpool were without Salah and Firmino. What followed has become Anfield legend:

MinuteGoalAggregate
7Divock Origi1-3
54Georginio Wijnaldum2-3
56Wijnaldum again3-3
79Origi, after Trent Alexander-Arnold's quick corner4-3

Alexander-Arnold noticed Barcelona's defenders turning away, took the corner before they were ready, and Origi swept it in. It's one of the sharpest pieces of thinking ever seen in a semi-final.

Anfield, where Liverpool overturned a 3-0 deficit against Barcelona. Photo: Arne Müseler, CC BY-SA 3.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Madrid: the final

The final against Tottenham was tense rather than spectacular. After two minutes, Moussa Sissoko was penalised for handball and Salah scored the penalty, getting the goal he had been denied in Kyiv. Alisson saved well as Spurs pressed, and Origi settled it in the 87th minute.

Mohamed Salah, who scored in the 2019 final. Photo: Bryan Berlin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Why it mattered

  • It came in a season when Liverpool won 97 Premier League points and still finished second to Manchester City by a single point.
  • It was the club's sixth European Cup, the most of any English club.
  • It started the most successful spell of Klopp's reign: the UEFA Super Cup and Club World Cup followed in 2019, and the Premier League title in 2019-20, Liverpool's first league championship in 30 years.

Kyiv taught Liverpool how big games are lost. Madrid showed they had learned.

Originally published on FootballHub.

posts.title: The miracle of Istanbul: how Liverpool won the 2005 Champions League from 3-0 down
posts.summary: Three goals behind at half-time against one of the greatest Milan sides ever, Liverpool scored three in six minutes and won on penalties. The full story of the Champions League's most famous comeback, and the season that led to it.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: The Atatürk Olympic Stadium in Istanbul, scene of the 2005 final. Photo: Валерий Дед, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

No Champions League final has been retold as often as Istanbul 2005. Liverpool were outplayed for 45 minutes, trailed 3-0 at half-time, and still went home with the trophy. To understand why it still matters to Liverpool fans, you have to start long before the night itself.

An unlikely season

Rafael Benítez arrived from Valencia in the summer of 2004. Liverpool hadn't won the league since 1990 and finished only fifth in the Premier League that season. Nobody expected a European run.

The campaign nearly ended in December. Liverpool needed to beat Olympiacos by two goals in their final group game. They were losing at half-time; then Florent Sinama Pongolle and Neil Mellor scored, and with four minutes left Steven Gerrard hit a dipping half-volley from the edge of the box to make it 3-1.

RoundOpponentAggregate
Last 16Bayer Leverkusen6-2
Quarter-finalJuventus2-1
Semi-finalChelsea1-0
FinalAC Milan3-3 (3-2 on penalties)

The semi-final against José Mourinho's Chelsea, who had just won the league, was decided by Luis García's early goal at Anfield, a shot that Chelsea still insist never crossed the line.

Steven Gerrard, Liverpool's captain in 2005. Photo: Эдгар Брещанов, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

The first half: 3-0

Milan were the favourites by a distance: Paolo Maldini, Andrea Pirlo, Kaká, Andriy Shevchenko and Hernán Crespo. Maldini volleyed in after less than a minute. Crespo scored twice just before half-time, the second from a sublime Kaká pass. At 3-0, the game looked finished.

Half-time: Benítez's change

In the dressing room, Benítez reorganised the team. He brought on midfielder Dietmar Hamann for right-back Steve Finnan and moved to three at the back, freeing Gerrard to push forward and giving Liverpool control of the middle of the pitch. In the stands, Liverpool's supporters sang "You'll Never Walk Alone" throughout the interval.

Six minutes

MinuteGoalScore
54Steven Gerrard heads in John Arne Riise's cross1-3
56Vladimír Šmicer from 25 yards2-3
60Xabi Alonso scores the rebound after his penalty is saved3-3

Gerrard's header, and his arms waving to the crowd as he ran back, changed the night. Two minutes later Šmicer's low shot beat Dida. Then Gerrard was brought down by Gennaro Gattuso, and Alonso followed in his own saved penalty.

Dudek

Milan dominated extra time. In the 117th minute Jerzy Dudek made a double save from Shevchenko at point-blank range, one of the most remarkable saves in a final.

In the shoot-out, Jamie Carragher told Dudek to copy Bruce Grobbelaar's wobbly-legged routine from the 1984 final. Dudek danced on his line, Serginho blazed over, Pirlo was saved, and when Dudek saved again from Shevchenko, Liverpool had won 3-2.

What it meant

It was Liverpool's fifth European Cup, which under UEFA's rules at the time meant they kept the trophy permanently. Because they had finished fifth in the league, UEFA let them defend the title the next season by entering from the very first qualifying round.

For a generation of fans, Istanbul became the proof that Liverpool were never beaten until the final whistle, an idea the club would lean on again in 2019.

posts.title: Jack Grealish and the treble: how a £100m entertainer became Guardiola's controller
posts.summary: Grealish arrived as English football's most expensive player and a flair dribbler, struggled in his first season, then reinvented himself as the left-sided winger who kept City's treble machine balanced. Here's what he actually did in 2022-23.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: Jack Grealish in Manchester City colours, July 2024. Photo: Hameltion, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

When Manchester City paid Aston Villa £100 million for Jack Grealish in August 2021, it was a British transfer record and a statement. Villa's captain was the most entertaining English player of his generation: socks rolled down, shoulders dropped, dribbling past defenders and winning fouls all over the pitch.

Two seasons later he was a treble winner. But the Grealish who lifted the Premier League, the FA Cup and the Champions League in 2022-23 was a different player from the one who arrived. Understanding how he changed explains a lot about how Pep Guardiola's best team worked.

The difficult first season

Grealish's first year at City was hard. At Villa every attack went through him, and he had the freedom to carry the ball wherever he wanted. At City he was one of many attackers in a system built on patience and positional discipline. He scored only three Premier League goals in 2021-22, and critics asked whether City had overpaid.

Villa Park, where Grealish grew up as a player and became Aston Villa captain. Photo: Arne Müseler, CC BY-SA 3.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

The problem wasn't talent. It was fit. Guardiola didn't need another player to dribble past three defenders; he needed someone who could do a very specific job on the left.

The job: control on the left

In 2022-23 City added Erling Haaland, and in the spring Guardiola moved John Stones into midfield to build a 3-2 base behind the attack. In that shape, the front five had clearly defined roles, and Grealish's was distinctive:

What Grealish didWhy it mattered
Stayed wide on the leftStretched the opposition's defence, opening space in the middle for De Bruyne, Gündoğan and Haaland
Kept the ball under pressureGave City a safe outlet; opponents struggled to take it off him
Drew foulsHe has long been one of the most-fouled players in the league, which relieved pressure and gave City free kicks
Slowed the game when neededLate in tight matches he took the ball to the corner flag and held it, running down the clock
Worked backTracked runners down City's left and pressed defenders, a part of his game that grew enormously

Guardiola's approach is built on control: keep the ball, limit chances, and never let the game become chaotic. Grealish became one of the clearest examples of that idea. He stopped trying to beat every defender and started choosing the moment, holding the ball to let team-mates move into position, then releasing it.

Pep Guardiola rebuilt Grealish's game around control rather than flair. Photo: Steffen Prößdorf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Balance on the left, danger on the right

City's attack was deliberately asymmetric. On the right, Kevin De Bruyne drifted into the half-space to deliver crosses and through balls. On the left, Grealish held his position wide. That balance meant that when City lost the ball, they were rarely exposed: players were already spread across the pitch in the right places to press or recover.

It also helped Haaland. With Grealish pinning the opposition's right-back wide, central defenders had less help, and Haaland had more room to attack crosses and runs in behind. Haaland scored 36 Premier League goals that season, a record.

The big nights

Grealish was a regular in the side through City's spring surge, when they overhauled Arsenal at the top of the table, and he played his part in the decisive matches of the treble:

  • The Champions League campaign, including the 4-0 semi-final second-leg win over Real Madrid at the Etihad, one of the most complete performances of the Guardiola era.
  • The FA Cup final against Manchester United at Wembley on 3 June 2023, won 2-1 with two goals from İlkay Gündoğan.
  • The Champions League final against Inter in Istanbul on 10 June 2023, won 1-0 through Rodri's second-half goal.

Wembley Stadium, where City beat United in the 2023 FA Cup final. Photo: Arne Müseler, CC BY-SA 3.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

In the final in Istanbul, City were not at their fluent best, and the game turned into a test of nerve. That was exactly the kind of match for which Grealish's new game was built: keep possession, win fouls, take the sting out of the opposition, and make sure nothing went wrong on the left.

The Atatürk Olympic Stadium in Istanbul, where City completed the treble. Photo: Валерий Дед, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

The celebrations

Grealish also became the face of the celebrations. His enthusiasm on the open-top bus parade through Manchester and in the days of partying that followed made him one of the defining images of the summer, a reminder that the system player still had the personality of the entertainer.

What the treble season says about him

Grealish's 2022-23 is a lesson in how great teams use great players. City didn't sign him to be the star; they reshaped his talent to serve the team. He gave up some of the things that made him famous, the long dribbles and the spectacular moments, and gained a role in one of the best club sides English football has seen.

Fans who remember the Villa captain might still wish he'd been let loose more often. But the medal count from that season is hard to argue with: a league title, an FA Cup and a Champions League, with Grealish on the left of the side that won them all.

posts.title: Football basics: formations and tactics for beginners
posts.summary: What 4-4-2, 4-3-3 and 3-5-2 actually mean, why teams press, what possession football is, and the tactical words commentators use, explained with Premier League examples.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: Pep Guardiola, whose possession-based tactics changed the Premier League. Photo: Steffen Prößdorf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Once you know the rules and the positions, tactics are what make football endlessly interesting. Every manager has a plan for how their team should attack, defend and switch between the two. This guide covers the ideas you'll hear about most.

Formations

A formation describes how a team's ten outfield players are arranged, counted from the back. The goalkeeper isn't included.

FormationShapeStrengths
4-4-2Four defenders, four midfielders, two strikersSimple, balanced, two lines of four that are hard to break down
4-3-3Four defenders, three midfielders, three forwardsWidth from wingers, control from a three-man midfield
4-2-3-1Two holding midfielders, a number 10 and two wide players behind one strikerSolid protection for the defence plus a creative playmaker
3-5-2Three centre-backs, wing-backs, three central midfielders, two strikersExtra cover at the back, wing-backs provide width

Formations are a starting point, not a fixed picture. Teams change shape constantly during a match: a 4-3-3 might look like a 3-2-5 when attacking and a 4-5-1 when defending.

Possession football

Some teams want the ball as much as possible. They pass patiently, move the opposition around and wait for an opening. Pep Guardiola's Manchester City are the best-known example: their 2017-18 side set records for points (100) and goals (106).

Pressing

Pressing means chasing the opponents in a coordinated group to win the ball back quickly, ideally high up the pitch near their goal. Jürgen Klopp's Liverpool became famous for it. A good press can create chances straight from the opponent's mistakes.

Jürgen Klopp, whose pressing Liverpool won the 2019 Champions League and the 2019-20 Premier League. Photo: Derivative work: EndzoneEnthusiast, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Counter-attacking

Some teams are happy to let the opponent have the ball, defend deep and compactly, then break forward at speed when they win it back. Leicester City won the 2015-16 title playing this way, with Jamie Vardy running behind defences.

Words you'll hear

  • High line: defenders push up towards halfway to keep the team compact. Risky against fast strikers.
  • Low block: a team defending deep near its own penalty area.
  • Overload: putting more players than the opponent in one area of the pitch.
  • Half-spaces: the channels between the middle and the sides, a favourite area for creative players.
  • Transition: the moment a team switches from defending to attacking, or the other way round.
  • Set pieces: corners, free kicks and throw-ins, often rehearsed in training.

How to watch tactically

  1. Count the defenders when the team has the ball. Many teams build with three at the back even if they defend with four.
  2. Watch the space between the lines. The best attacking players find pockets between the opposition's midfield and defence.
  3. Look at what happens after losing the ball. Does the team press immediately or drop back into shape?

That completes the Football basics series. Now pick a club, watch a match, and see how many of these ideas you can spot.

posts.title: Football basics: how the Premier League season works
posts.summary: Twenty clubs, 38 matches, three points for a win. How the table works, what goal difference means, who goes up and down, how clubs qualify for Europe, and what transfer windows are.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: Old Trafford, one of 20 Premier League grounds. Photo: Arne Müseler from Salzburg, AT, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

The Premier League is England's top division and the most watched football league in the world. Its season can look complicated from the outside, with tables, points, goal difference and promotion, but it follows a simple pattern.

The format

  • 20 clubs.
  • Each club plays every other club twice, once at home and once away.
  • That's 38 matches per club, running from August to May.
  • Teams usually play once a week, at weekends, with some midweek rounds.

Points and the table

ResultPoints
Win3
Draw1
Defeat0

The league table ranks clubs by points. When clubs finish level on points, they are separated by:

  1. Goal difference: goals scored minus goals conceded.
  2. Goals scored.
  3. Then their results against each other.

Goal difference really matters. Manchester City won the 2011-12 title on goal difference after finishing level with Manchester United on 89 points.

What a club is playing for

  • First place: the club with most points is champion and lifts the trophy.
  • The top places qualify for European competitions the next season, mainly the Champions League for the top four. Extra places can come from cup wins and from how well English clubs have done in Europe that season.
  • The bottom three are relegated to the Championship, the second tier of English football.

Every season, 380 Premier League matches kick off between August and May. Photo: Michael Barera, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Promotion and relegation

English football is a pyramid of linked divisions. Three clubs come up from the Championship each season: the top two automatically, plus the winner of a play-off between the clubs finishing third to sixth. Relegation is a huge financial blow, which is why the battle to avoid the bottom three can be as dramatic as the title race.

Cups alongside the league

Clubs also play knockout cup competitions during the season:

  • FA Cup: the oldest football competition in the world, open to hundreds of clubs from every level of the pyramid.
  • League Cup: for the 92 clubs in the Premier League and English Football League.
  • European competitions: the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League, for clubs that qualified.

Winning the league, the FA Cup and the Champions League in the same season is called the treble. Manchester United did it in 1999 and Manchester City in 2023.

Transfer windows

Clubs can only sign players from other clubs during two transfer windows: a long one in the summer and a shorter one in January. Outside those windows, squads are mostly fixed.

Reading a league table

ColumnMeans
PPlayed
W / D / LWon, drawn, lost
GF / GAGoals for, goals against
GDGoal difference
PtsPoints

posts.title: Football basics: fouls, free kicks, penalties and cards
posts.summary: What counts as a foul, the difference between a direct and an indirect free kick, when a penalty is given, what yellow and red cards mean, and how the advantage rule keeps the game flowing.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: A free kick: the defending wall must stand at least 9.15 metres away. Photo: photo taken by Markus Dallarosa, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Football is a contact sport, but there are limits. When a player crosses them, the referee awards a free kick or a penalty, and may show a card. Here's how it works.

What counts as a foul

A foul is when a player, against an opponent and while the ball is in play:

  • kicks, trips, pushes, charges, strikes or jumps at them carelessly, recklessly or with excessive force;
  • holds them or their shirt;
  • makes a tackle and catches the player instead of the ball;
  • deliberately handles the ball (or makes their body unnaturally bigger with their arm and the ball hits it).

Free kicks

The team that was fouled gets a free kick from where the foul happened. Opponents must stand at least 9.15 metres (10 yards) away, which is why defenders form a wall for free kicks near goal.

TypeWhenCan you score directly?
Direct free kickMost fouls, including handballYes
Indirect free kickOffside, dangerous play without contact, obstructing an opponentNo: another player must touch it first. The referee raises an arm until it's touched

Penalties

A penalty kick: one shot from 11 metres against the goalkeeper. Photo: IQRemix from Canada, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

If the defending team commits a direct-free-kick foul inside its own penalty area, the attackers get a penalty: one shot from the penalty spot, 11 metres from goal, with only the goalkeeper to beat. Everyone else must stand outside the area until the kick is taken. The goalkeeper must have at least part of one foot on the goal line when the ball is kicked.

Cards

A referee shows a card. Photo: Mehdi Bolourian, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

CardMeaningTypical reasons
YellowA caution (booking)A reckless foul, persistent fouling, time-wasting, dissent, stopping a promising attack
Second yellowBecomes a redTwo cautions in one match
RedSent off immediatelySerious foul play, violent conduct, denying an obvious goal-scoring opportunity, offensive language

A player who is sent off leaves the pitch and can't be replaced, so the team plays with one fewer for the rest of the match. In the Premier League a red card also brings a suspension for following matches, and collecting too many yellow cards over a season leads to a ban too.

Advantage

If a team is fouled but still has a good attacking chance, the referee can let play continue and shout "advantage!", stretching both arms forward. Stopping for a free kick would only help the team that committed the foul. The referee can still show a card when play next stops.

Dissent and captains

Players who protest decisions aggressively can be booked for dissent. Referees increasingly speak only to captains about decisions, to stop crowds of players surrounding the officials.

posts.title: Football basics: the offside rule, explained simply
posts.summary: The rule that confuses new fans more than any other, in plain language. When a player is offside, when they aren't, the exceptions, and why the rule exists at all.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: An assistant referee flags for offside. Photo: Steindy (talk) 23:45, 26 November 2010 (UTC), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

If football has one famously confusing rule, it's offside. The good news is that it comes down to one question, asked at one moment. Once you know the question, you'll be able to call offsides from the sofa.

Why the rule exists

Without offside, a team could leave a striker standing next to the other team's goalkeeper all game, waiting for long balls. Offside forces attackers to stay roughly level with the defence until the ball is played, which keeps the game compact and makes attacking a matter of timing and movement.

The one question

At the moment a team-mate plays or touches the ball, ask:

Is the attacker closer to the opponents' goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent?

If yes, they are in an offside position.

  • The second-last opponent is usually the last outfield defender, because the goalkeeper is normally the last.
  • What counts is the attacker's head, body and feet. Arms and hands don't count, because players can't legally play the ball with them.
  • Level is onside. If any part of the attacker that can score is level with the defender, they're fine.

Being in an offside position isn't enough

This is the part most people miss. Standing in an offside position isn't an offence. It only becomes offside if the attacker then gets involved in play, by:

  1. Playing or touching the ball passed to them.
  2. Interfering with an opponent, for example blocking the goalkeeper's view or challenging a defender for the ball.
  3. Gaining an advantage, such as collecting a rebound off the post or the goalkeeper.

A player standing offside on the far side of the pitch, nowhere near the action, isn't penalised.

The exceptions

You can't be offside:

  • in your own half of the pitch;
  • directly from a throw-in, a goal kick or a corner kick;
  • if you are level with or behind the ball when it's played.

What happens when it's given

The assistant referee raises their flag, the referee stops play, and the defending team gets an indirect free kick from where the offence happened.

VAR reviews offside decisions before a goal is confirmed. Photo: Carlos Figueroa, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Offside and VAR

Offside is judged at the exact moment of the pass, often with players moving fast in opposite directions, so it's one of the hardest calls to make live. Assistant referees are now often told to keep their flag down in tight situations and let play continue; if a goal is scored, the video assistant referee checks the moment of the pass with lines drawn on the replay.

Three examples

SituationDecision
Striker is a step behind the last defender when the pass is played, then sprints past him to scoreGoal. Onside at the moment of the pass.
Striker is a step beyond the last defender when the pass is playedOffside, once he plays the ball.
Winger is beyond the defence on the far side, not involved, while a team-mate scores from a shotGoal. Being in an offside position isn't an offence unless you're involved.
