posts.title: Football basics: every position on the pitch explained
posts.summary: Goalkeeper, centre-back, full-back, holding midfielder, number 10, winger, striker. What each player is for, what makes a good one, and Premier League players who show how it's done.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: Goalkeeper Alisson Becker playing for Brazil in 2026. Photo: Bryan Berlin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Every team has eleven players, but they are not interchangeable. Each position has a job, and understanding those jobs is the quickest way to understand what you're watching. Players are often described by shirt numbers that traditionally went with each role, so you'll hear commentators talk about a "number 6" or a "number 9".

Goalkeeper (number 1)

The last line of defence and the only player allowed to handle the ball, inside their own penalty area. A goalkeeper needs reflexes to make saves, courage to come off their line for crosses, and today, good feet: modern teams expect the keeper to start attacks with accurate passes.

Defenders

Centre-backs (numbers 4 and 5)

The central defenders. Their job is to stop the other team's strikers: marking, tackling, winning headers and blocking shots. The best are calm on the ball too, passing out of defence under pressure.

Virgil van Dijk, a model modern centre-back, playing for the Netherlands. Photo: Ailura, CC BY-SA 3.0 at, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Full-backs (numbers 2 and 3)

The defenders on the right and left. They defend against wingers, but also overlap down the sides to cross the ball. In a back three, they push further forward and become wing-backs. Some modern full-backs move into midfield when their team has the ball, a role called the inverted full-back.

Midfielders

Defensive midfielder (number 6)

Sits just in front of the defence. Breaks up attacks, protects the centre-backs and recycles possession with simple passes. Manchester City's Rodri, who won the 2024 Ballon d'Or, is the textbook example.

Central midfielders (number 8)

The engine of the team, covering ground in both directions: pressing, passing, tackling and arriving in the penalty area to score.

Declan Rice, an all-action central midfielder, playing for England in 2026. Photo: Bryan Berlin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Attacking midfielder (number 10)

Plays in the space between the opposition's midfield and defence. The creative heart of the team, providing the final pass for strikers. Kevin De Bruyne and Martin Ødegaard have played versions of this role.

Forwards

Wingers (numbers 7 and 11)

Wide attackers who beat defenders with dribbling and speed, cross the ball, and often cut inside onto their stronger foot to shoot. Mohamed Salah and Bukayo Saka have been among the league's best.

Winger Bukayo Saka playing for England in 2026. Photo: Bryan Berlin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Striker (number 9)

The main goalscorer, leading the line in the middle. Some strikers are powerful targets who win headers; others are fast runners behind the defence. Erling Haaland's 36 goals in 2022-23 set the Premier League record for a season.

A false nine is a striker who drops deep into midfield instead of staying up front, pulling defenders out of position for others to exploit.

Quick reference

PositionShort nameMain job
GoalkeeperGKStop shots, start attacks
Centre-backCBStop the opposition's strikers
Full-back / wing-backRB, LB, RWB, LWBDefend the flanks, support attacks
Defensive midfielderDMProtect the defence, keep the ball moving
Central midfielderCMLink defence and attack
Attacking midfielderAMCreate chances
WingerRW, LWBeat defenders, cross, cut inside
StrikerST, CFScore goals

Next in the series: the offside rule, the one that confuses everyone.

posts.title: Football basics: the rules of the game in ten minutes
posts.summary: Never watched a full match? Start here. What the players are trying to do, how a goal counts, how long a game lasts, and the handful of rules that explain almost everything you'll see.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: A match in progress: two teams, one ball, two goals. Photo: Rick Dikeman, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Football (called soccer in some countries) is the world's most popular sport, and its basic idea is simple: get the ball into the other team's goal more often than they get it into yours. Here is everything a newcomer needs to follow a match.

The aim

Two teams of eleven players each defend one goal and attack the other. Players move the ball with their feet, head and body, but not their hands or arms. The only exception is the goalkeeper, who may handle the ball inside their own penalty area.

A goal counts when the whole of the ball crosses the whole of the goal line between the posts and under the crossbar. The team with more goals wins. If the scores are level, the match is a draw.

The pitch

The markings of a football pitch. Photo: snater.com, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Pitches are rectangles of grass, around 105 metres long and 68 metres wide at Premier League grounds. The most important markings:

  • Halfway line: splits the pitch; each team starts in its own half.
  • Penalty area: the large box in front of each goal. The goalkeeper can use their hands here, and a foul by defenders here gives a penalty.
  • Goal area: the small box, where goal kicks are taken.
  • Penalty spot: 11 metres (12 yards) from the goal.

How long a match lasts

PartLength
First half45 minutes
Half-time15 minutes
Second half45 minutes
Stoppage timeA few minutes added at the end of each half for delays

The clock never stops, so the referee adds stoppage time (also called added time) for injuries, substitutions, goal celebrations and time-wasting. In knockout cup ties that end level, there is extra time (two halves of 15 minutes) and, if still level, a penalty shoot-out.

The team

Each side starts with 11 players: one goalkeeper and ten outfield players, usually split into defenders, midfielders and forwards. In the Premier League each team may make five substitutions from a bench of nine. A player who is substituted can't come back on.

The ten rules that explain most of a match

  1. Kick-off starts each half and restarts play after a goal.
  2. Throw-in when the ball crosses a sideline. It's thrown with both hands from behind the head.
  3. Goal kick when an attacker puts the ball over the goal line (outside the goal).
  4. Corner kick when a defender puts it over their own goal line.
  5. Fouls (tripping, pushing, kicking, holding, deliberate handball) give a free kick to the other team.
  6. A foul by defenders in their own penalty area gives a penalty.
  7. A yellow card is a warning; two yellows or a red card means the player is sent off and the team plays a player short.
  8. Offside stops attackers from waiting behind the defence. It has its own guide in this series.
  9. The referee has the final word, helped by two assistants on the sidelines and a video assistant referee (VAR) for big decisions.
  10. Advantage: if stopping play would hurt the team that was fouled, the referee lets the game flow.

The referee controls the match and applies the Laws of the Game. Photo: Эдгар Брещанов, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Results and points

In a league, a win earns 3 points, a draw 1 point and a defeat none. Over a season those points decide the table, which the guide to how the Premier League works explains.

What to watch for in your first match

  • Where the ball is won back. Teams that win the ball high up the pitch usually create more chances.
  • Shape without the ball. Watch how the defenders and midfielders move together as a unit.
  • Set pieces. A big share of goals come from corners and free kicks.

Next in the series: what every position on the pitch actually does.

posts.title: 6-1 and 93:20: the season Manchester City found a new generation of fans
posts.summary: The derby thrashing at Old Trafford, an eight-point gap with six games left, and Sergio Agüero's winner against QPR in the 94th minute. How 2011-12 turned "typical City" into champions and created a new generation of supporters.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: The statue of Sergio Agüero outside the Etihad Stadium, unveiled ten years after his goal against QPR. Photo: Christian David, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

For most of their history, being a Manchester City fan meant learning to expect the worst. Supporters even had a phrase for it: "typical City", the habit of finding a way to lose from a winning position. Their last league title had come in 1968. Their neighbours across the city won it almost every year.

In one season, 2011-12, that changed. Two afternoons in particular, a 6-1 win at Old Trafford in October and a 3-2 win over Queens Park Rangers in May, rewrote what it meant to support City. For a generation of younger fans they were the moment the club became theirs.

Before: noisy neighbours

In September 2008 the Abu Dhabi United Group, led by Sheikh Mansour, bought the club. Money arrived, but so did mockery. When City put up a "Welcome to Manchester" billboard after signing Carlos Tevez from United in 2009, Sir Alex Ferguson dismissed them as "noisy neighbours".

Roberto Mancini, who managed City from December 2009 to 2013. Photo: M.Sadegh Nikgostar, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Roberto Mancini replaced Mark Hughes in December 2009 and built a side that could defend. In 2011 City beat United 1-0 in the FA Cup semi-final and Stoke 1-0 in the final, both through Yaya Touré goals. It was the club's first major trophy since the 1976 League Cup, and that summer they signed a 23-year-old striker from Atlético Madrid called Sergio Agüero.

23 October 2011: six at Old Trafford

City arrived at Old Trafford top of the league. They left having handed United one of the heaviest defeats in the club's history.

MinuteEventScore
22Mario BalotelliUnited 0-1 City
47Jonny Evans sent off
60Balotelli again0-2
69Sergio Agüero0-3
81Darren Fletcher1-3
89Edin Džeko1-4
90+1Džeko1-5
90+3David Silva1-6

Old Trafford, where City won 6-1 in October 2011. Photo: Arne Müseler from Salzburg, AT, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

After his first goal, Balotelli lifted his shirt to show a T-shirt reading "Why always me?", one of the defining images of the season. United were down to ten men and chasing the game when City scored three times in the last few minutes. It was United's heaviest home defeat since 1955, and Ferguson called it the worst result of his career.

Mario Balotelli scored twice at Old Trafford and later set up the most famous goal in Premier League history. Photo: Amirhosseinnakhaeii, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

The scoreline mattered beyond the three points. In a title race eventually decided on goal difference, those five extra goals at Old Trafford turned out to be worth a championship.

April 2012: eight points behind

City led for much of the season, then stumbled in the spring. After losing 1-0 at Arsenal on 8 April they were eight points behind United with six games left. Mancini said publicly that the title race was over.

Then United wobbled. They lost 1-0 at Wigan, then threw away a 4-2 lead to draw 4-4 with Everton at Old Trafford. On 30 April the two clubs met at the Etihad with City three points behind but with a better goal difference. Just before half-time, captain Vincent Kompany headed in David Silva's corner. City won 1-0 and went top on goal difference.

The statue of captain Vincent Kompany at the Etihad Stadium. Photo: Christian David, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

A 2-0 win at Newcastle, with two more goals from Yaya Touré, left City needing to beat QPR at home on the final day.

13 May 2012: 93:20

QPR were fighting relegation, and City were expected to win comfortably. Pablo Zabaleta put them ahead just before half-time. Then it fell apart in the most "typical City" way imaginable.

MinuteEventScore
39Pablo ZabaletaCity 1-0 QPR
48Djibril Cissé1-1
55Joey Barton sent off
66Jamie Mackie, for ten-man QPR1-2
90+2Edin Džeko header2-2
90+4 (93:20)Sergio Agüero3-2

At Sunderland, United won 1-0 through Wayne Rooney. Their game finished first, and as the Etihad match went into stoppage time with City losing, United were champions. Their players waited on the pitch at the Stadium of Light for the final score.

Edin Džeko's header in the 92nd minute made it 2-2. Photo: Ailura, CC BY-SA 3.0 at, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Džeko headed in Silva's corner to make it 2-2. Two minutes later Agüero played the ball into Balotelli, collected the return, skipped past a sliding challenge and drove it past goalkeeper Paddy Kenny. The clock read 93 minutes and 20 seconds. On Sky, commentator Martin Tyler screamed "Agüerooooo!" and told viewers they would never see anything like it again.

City and United both finished on 89 points. City won the title on goal difference, +64 to +56. It was their first league title in 44 years.

Sergio Agüero, scorer of the winner against QPR. Photo: Кирилл Венедиктов, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

The new generation

The trophy was the headline, but the bigger change was in the stands and in school playgrounds.

  • A new identity. "Typical City" stopped meaning collapse. A whole generation of younger supporters grew up with 93:20 as their first big memory of the club, not decades of disappointment.
  • A city split differently. For years, children in Manchester had grown up surrounded by United's success. After 2012 there were two clubs worth choosing, and many chose sky blue.
  • A global audience. The goal was replayed around the world and is regularly voted among the greatest moments in Premier League history. It gave City a story that attracted new supporters abroad, at exactly the time the club was building its international profile.
  • A foundation for more. The 2012 title was the first of eight Premier League titles by 2024, including four in a row under Pep Guardiola.

The Etihad Stadium, where 93:20 changed what it meant to support City. Photo: Arne Müseler, cropped by Blackcat, CC BY-SA 3.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Ten years after the goal, in 2022, City unveiled a statue of Agüero outside the Etihad, alongside statues of Kompany and Silva.

Why it still matters

City's later sides were better. Guardiola's teams set records that the 2012 side never came close to. But no title meant as much, because none was won from as far behind, against the rival that mattered most, and in such an unlikely way. The 6-1 announced that the noisy neighbours could win at Old Trafford. The 93:20 proved they could win the league. Together they turned a club defined by disappointment into one defined by belief, and gave a new generation of fans a reason to choose blue.

Originally published on FootballHub.

posts.title: From Barcelona to Istanbul: how Premier League clubs conquered the Champions League
posts.summary: Seven titles and sixteen finals since 1992, two miracles in Istanbul and three all-English finals. The full story of England's top flight in Europe's biggest competition.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: The Atatürk Olympic Stadium in Istanbul, where Liverpool won in 2005 and Manchester City in 2023. Photo: Валерий Дед, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

When the Premier League began in 1992, English football was still recovering from the ban that kept its clubs out of Europe after the Heysel disaster in 1985. In the three decades since, Premier League clubs have reached the Champions League final sixteen times and won it seven times. Few competitions have produced as many unforgettable English nights.

The scoreboard

Counting the old European Cup as well, English clubs have won Europe's top prize 15 times.

ClubEuropean Cups / Champions LeaguesYears wonFinals in the Premier League era
Liverpool61977, 1978, 1981, 1984, 2005, 20195 (2005, 2007, 2018, 2019, 2022)
Manchester United31968, 1999, 20084 (1999, 2008, 2009, 2011)
Chelsea22012, 20213 (2008, 2012, 2021)
Nottingham Forest21979, 1980none
Aston Villa11982none
Manchester City120232 (2021, 2023)
Arsenal0none1 (2006)
Tottenham Hotspur0none1 (2019)

The seven Premier League-era triumphs

1999, Manchester United 2-1 Bayern Munich (Barcelona). United trailed going into stoppage time at Camp Nou. Teddy Sheringham equalised, then Ole Gunnar Solskjær poked in the winner two minutes later. It completed the treble of league, FA Cup and European Cup.

Ole Gunnar Solskjær, scorer of United's injury-time winner in the 1999 final. Photo: Tor Atle Kleven, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

2005, Liverpool 3-3 AC Milan, Liverpool won 3-2 on penalties (Istanbul). Milan led 3-0 at half-time. In six minutes Steven Gerrard, Vladimír Šmicer and Xabi Alonso levelled it, and Jerzy Dudek saved Andriy Shevchenko's penalty in the shoot-out. It is still the comeback every other comeback is measured against.

2008, Manchester United 1-1 Chelsea, United won 6-5 on penalties (Moscow). The first all-English final, played in the rain at the Luzhniki. John Terry slipped and hit the post with the kick that would have won it for Chelsea, and Edwin van der Sar saved from Nicolas Anelka.

2012, Chelsea 1-1 Bayern Munich, Chelsea won 4-3 on penalties (Munich). Bayern were at home and in control. Didier Drogba headed an 88th-minute equaliser, Petr Čech saved Arjen Robben's penalty in extra time, and Drogba scored the final kick of the shoot-out.

Didier Drogba, who equalised and scored the winning penalty in 2012. Photo: Y.Leclercq©, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

2019, Liverpool 2-0 Tottenham Hotspur (Madrid). Mohamed Salah scored a penalty in the second minute and Divock Origi sealed it late. Liverpool had reached the final with a 4-0 win over Barcelona at Anfield after losing the first leg 3-0.

2021, Chelsea 1-0 Manchester City (Porto). Kai Havertz ran through and scored just before half-time. Thomas Tuchel had taken over in January and beaten Pep Guardiola three times in six weeks.

2023, Manchester City 1-0 Inter (Istanbul). Rodri's 68th-minute strike won City their first Champions League and completed a treble, eighteen years after Liverpool's miracle in the same stadium.

The ones that got away

England's nine lost finals since 1992 tell their own story: Arsenal against Barcelona in 2006 after Jens Lehmann was sent off; Liverpool against Milan in 2007; Manchester United outplayed by Pep Guardiola's Barcelona in 2009 and 2011; Liverpool beaten by Real Madrid in 2018 and 2022; and the losers of the three all-English finals.

What changed

Three things explain the rise:

  • Money. Television deals from the late 1990s onwards let English clubs sign the best players in the world.
  • Coaching. Sir Alex Ferguson, Rafael Benítez, Jürgen Klopp, Thomas Tuchel and Guardiola all won the trophy in England, bringing tactical ideas that the league then copied.
  • Depth. In 2019 both European finals were all-English (Liverpool v Tottenham, and Chelsea v Arsenal in the Europa League), the clearest sign of how strong the league had become.

Mohamed Salah, who scored in the 2019 final in Madrid. Photo: Bryan Berlin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

The Champions League has grown into a 36-team league phase since 2024-25, which means more Premier League nights against Europe's elite every season. The record says English clubs will keep turning up on the last night in May.

posts.title: Shearer, Henry, Kane, Salah, Haaland: the Premier League's great strikers compared
posts.summary: The all-time scorers, the Golden Boot kings and the single-season records, with the numbers side by side. Who really was the best finisher of the Premier League era?
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: Erling Haaland, whose 36 goals in 2022-23 set the single-season record. Photo: Bryan Berlin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Every era of the Premier League has had a striker who defined it. Alan Shearer in the 1990s, Thierry Henry in the 2000s, Sergio Agüero and Harry Kane in the 2010s, Mohamed Salah and Erling Haaland since. Comparing them across different teams and decades is never perfect, but the numbers give a solid place to start.

The all-time scorers

Premier League goals, as of the end of the 2024-25 season:

RankPlayerGoalsMain clubs
1Alan Shearer260Blackburn Rovers, Newcastle United
2Harry Kane213Tottenham Hotspur
3Wayne Rooney208Everton, Manchester United
4Andrew Cole187Newcastle United, Manchester United
5Mohamed Salah186Liverpool
6Sergio Agüero184Manchester City
7Frank Lampard177Chelsea
8Thierry Henry175Arsenal
9Robbie Fowler163Liverpool
10Jermain Defoe162Tottenham Hotspur

Shearer's 260 has stood for two decades. Kane looked the likeliest to catch him until he joined Bayern Munich in 2023.

Alan Shearer, the Premier League's record scorer. Photo: Originally carltonreid; retouched by DFS454, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Golden Boot kings

PlayerGolden BootsSeasons
Thierry Henry42001-02, 2003-04, 2004-05, 2005-06
Mohamed Salah42017-18, 2018-19 (shared), 2021-22 (shared), 2024-25
Alan Shearer31994-95, 1995-96, 1996-97
Harry Kane32015-16, 2016-17, 2020-21
Erling Haaland22022-23, 2023-24

Single-season records

  • Most goals in a season: Erling Haaland, 36 in 2022-23, his first season in England.
  • Before Haaland: Andrew Cole (1993-94) and Alan Shearer (1994-95) scored 34 each, but in 42-game seasons. Salah's 32 in 2017-18 was the 38-game record until Haaland.
  • Most hat-tricks: Sergio Agüero, 12.
  • Fastest hat-trick: Sadio Mané, 2 minutes 56 seconds against Aston Villa in 2015.

Thierry Henry, four-time Golden Boot winner. Photo: Web Summit, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Comparing the styles

Shearer was the complete centre-forward: power in the air, a ferocious shot and relentless penalty-box movement. He scored 30-plus league goals in three straight seasons.

Henry started wide and drifted, and he created as much as he scored. He also holds a share of the single-season assist record (20 in 2002-03), which makes his goal tally even more remarkable.

Kane turned himself into a number nine and a playmaker at once, dropping deep to pass while still finishing at an elite rate.

Salah changed what a wide forward could do. Starting from the right, he scored more league goals than any Liverpool player of the Premier League era.

Haaland is the purest finisher of the group: fewer touches, more goals, and records broken within months of arriving.

The verdict

If longevity matters most, Shearer still leads. If peak scoring matters most, Haaland's 36 is the number to beat. If you want the player who did everything, Henry's mix of goals, assists and trophies is hard to argue with. That's the point of a debate like this: the numbers narrow it down, and the rest is taste.

posts.title: Midfield masters: the players who ran the Premier League
posts.summary: Giggs's assists, Lampard's goals, Gerrard's big nights and the anchors who made it all possible. The greatest midfielders of the Premier League era, with the records to back them up.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: Paul Scholes, the passer every great midfielder named as the best. Photo: James Adams, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Strikers get the headlines, but Premier League titles have usually been won in midfield. The best teams of the last three decades were built around players who could pass, press, score and control a game. Here are the ones who stand out, and what they did that nobody else could.

The record books

RecordPlayerNumber
Most Premier League assistsRyan Giggs162
Second most assistsKevin De Bruyne119
Most goals by a midfielderFrank Lampard177
Most assists in a seasonThierry Henry (2002-03) and Kevin De Bruyne (2019-20)20
Most Premier League titlesRyan Giggs13

Cesc Fàbregas (111), Wayne Rooney (103) and Lampard (102) complete the list of players with more than 100 Premier League assists.

The goalscorers

Frank Lampard timed his runs into the box better than anyone. His 177 league goals from midfield put him seventh on the all-time scoring list, above most strikers in history.

Frank Lampard, the highest-scoring midfielder in Premier League history. Photo: Mehdi Bolourian, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Steven Gerrard scored 120 Premier League goals and owned the biggest occasions, from the Istanbul comeback in 2005 to the 2006 FA Cup final. The league title was the only major club prize he never won.

Yaya Touré scored 20 league goals in 2013-14 as Manchester City won the title, a return almost no central midfielder has matched.

The creators

Ryan Giggs played in the Premier League from its first season to 2014, won 13 titles and made 162 assists, both records.

Paul Scholes scored 107 league goals but is remembered most for his passing. Xavi, Zinedine Zidane and others named him as the midfielder they most admired.

Cesc Fàbregas made his debut as a teenager at Arsenal and later won two titles with Chelsea, passing his way to 111 assists.

Kevin De Bruyne combined vision and power like nobody else, and his 119 assists rank behind only Giggs.

The ball-winners

Patrick Vieira captained Arsenal's Invincibles, who went the whole 2003-04 season unbeaten.

Patrick Vieira, captain of Arsenal's unbeaten 2003-04 side. Photo: Simon Heseltine, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Roy Keane led Manchester United through their most dominant years, including the 1999 treble, although suspension kept him out of the Champions League final.

N'Golo Kanté won back-to-back titles with two different clubs, Leicester City in 2015-16 and Chelsea in 2016-17.

Rodri anchored Manchester City's four titles in a row and won the Ballon d'Or in 2024.

How midfield has changed

The 1990s and 2000s favoured box-to-box players who could do everything. Since the 2010s, coaches such as Pep Guardiola have split the job: a deep controller like Rodri, and creators like De Bruyne higher up. Whatever the system, the lesson of three decades is the same. Win the midfield and you usually win the league.

posts.title: The managers who won the Premier League, and how they did it
posts.summary: Only twelve managers have lifted the Premier League trophy. From Ferguson's thirteen titles to Ranieri's 5,000-1 miracle, here is every title-winning manager and what made each of them different.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: Sir Alex Ferguson, winner of 13 Premier League titles. Photo: Austin Osuide, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

From the first season in 1992-93 to 2024-25, only twelve managers won the Premier League. Some built dynasties, some won once and moved on, and one pulled off the most unlikely title in the history of sport.

Every title-winning manager

ManagerTitlesClub(s)Seasons
Sir Alex Ferguson13Manchester United1992-93, 1993-94, 1995-96, 1996-97, 1998-99, 1999-2000, 2000-01, 2002-03, 2006-07, 2007-08, 2008-09, 2010-11, 2012-13
Pep Guardiola6Manchester City2017-18, 2018-19, 2020-21, 2021-22, 2022-23, 2023-24
Arsène Wenger3Arsenal1997-98, 2001-02, 2003-04
José Mourinho3Chelsea2004-05, 2005-06, 2014-15
Kenny Dalglish1Blackburn Rovers1994-95
Carlo Ancelotti1Chelsea2009-10
Roberto Mancini1Manchester City2011-12
Manuel Pellegrini1Manchester City2013-14
Claudio Ranieri1Leicester City2015-16
Antonio Conte1Chelsea2016-17
Jürgen Klopp1Liverpool2019-20
Arne Slot1Liverpool2024-25

The dynasty builders

Sir Alex Ferguson won 13 of the first 21 Premier League titles. His real skill was renewal: he rebuilt United several times, from the Class of '92 to Cristiano Ronaldo and Wayne Rooney, and won three in a row twice. He added two Champions Leagues, in 1999 and 2008.

Pep Guardiola won six titles in seven seasons, including four in a row, which no team had done before. His City side set the records for points (100) and goals (106) in 2017-18.

Pep Guardiola, the only manager to win four Premier League titles in a row. Photo: Steffen Prößdorf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

The revolutionaries

Arsène Wenger changed English football's habits, from diet and fitness to scouting abroad. His 2003-04 Arsenal side went the whole season unbeaten, the Invincibles.

Arsène Wenger, whose Arsenal went unbeaten through 2003-04. Photo: Barcex, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

José Mourinho arrived at Chelsea in 2004 calling himself "a special one" and backed it up: 95 points and only 15 goals conceded in his first season, a defensive record that still stands.

Jürgen Klopp brought heavy-metal pressing to Liverpool, won the Champions League in 2019, then the club's first league title in 30 years in 2019-20 with 99 points.

The one-season wonders

Claudio Ranieri's Leicester City started 2015-16 as 5,000-1 outsiders and won the league by ten points, built on Jamie Vardy, Riyad Mahrez and N'Golo Kanté.

Carlo Ancelotti won the double with Chelsea in 2009-10, scoring a then-record 103 league goals.

Arne Slot won the title in his first season, 2024-25, after taking over from Klopp, and Liverpool clinched it with four games to spare.

What the winners share

Very different personalities, but the same pattern: a clear idea of how to play, players who fit it, and the authority to change things before they went stale. That last part is why Ferguson and Guardiola stand apart. They kept winning while changing their teams around them.

posts.title: Who rules the Premier League era? The most successful clubs since 1992
posts.summary: Title counts, record seasons and the six clubs that have never been relegated. A club-by-club look at who has dominated English football's top flight since the Premier League began.

Cover photo: Old Trafford, home of the Premier League's most successful club. Photo: Arne Müseler from Salzburg, AT, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Thirty-three Premier League seasons, from 1992-93 to 2024-25, produced only seven different champions. Here's how the honours are shared out, and the seasons that set the records.

Arsenal's unbeaten run eventually stretched to 49 league games, from May 2003 to October 2004.

Anfield, where Liverpool ended a 30-year wait for the league title in 2020. Photo: Arne Müseler, CC BY-SA 3.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

The ever-presents

Six clubs have played in every Premier League season: Arsenal, Chelsea, Everton, Liverpool, Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur. Everton and Tottenham are the two of those six that have never won it.

The great surprises

Blackburn Rovers (1994-95) were funded by local steel owner Jack Walker and led by Kenny Dalglish and Alan Shearer. They won the title on the final day despite losing at Anfield.

Leicester City (2015-16) were nearly relegated the season before and started as 5,000-1 outsiders. They won by ten points.

The King Power Stadium, home of Leicester City's 5,000-1 champions. Photo: Arne Müseler, CC BY-SA 3.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

The pattern

The Premier League has had dominant eras rather than an even spread: United in the 1990s and 2000s, Chelsea's spells after 2004, and City's run under Pep Guardiola. Money matters, but so does stability. Every long period of dominance came with a manager who stayed long enough to build something: Ferguson, Wenger, Guardiola and Klopp.

posts.title: Ferguson's United vs Guardiola's City: which was the greater dynasty?
posts.summary: Thirteen titles over two decades against six in seven years and four in a row. We put the two great Premier League dynasties side by side, trophy by trophy and record by record.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: Sir Alex Ferguson, who managed Manchester United from 1986 to 2013. Photo: Austin Osuide, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Manchester has been home to the two longest periods of dominance in Premier League history. Sir Alex Ferguson's Manchester United won 13 titles between 1993 and 2013. Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won six in seven seasons between 2018 and 2024, including four in a row. Which was greater?

Side by side

Ferguson's United (Premier League era)Guardiola's City
Premier League titles13 in 21 seasons6 in his first 8 seasons
Most in a row3 (twice: 1999-2001 and 2007-09)4 (2021-2024)
Champions Leagues2 (1999, 2008)1 (2023)
Trebles19992023
Record seasons92 points (1993-94, 42 games)100 points and 106 goals (2017-18)
Domestic clean sweep League, FA Cup and League Cup (2018-19)

The case for Ferguson

Longevity. Ferguson won titles across three different decades with almost completely different squads, from Eric Cantona and the Class of '92 to Cristiano Ronaldo, Wayne Rooney and Robin van Persie. Being on top for twenty years is a different achievement from being on top for seven.

Competition. His teams beat Blackburn, Arsenal's Invincibles era, Mourinho's Chelsea and the first City title side. He was never facing a single rival for long.

Europe. Two Champions Leagues, including the 1999 comeback in Barcelona, against Guardiola's one with City.

Old Trafford, where Ferguson's United won 13 Premier League titles. Photo: Arne Müseler from Salzburg, AT, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

The case for Guardiola

Peak level. No English team has played at City's standard. The 100-point season, the 2018-19 domestic treble and four titles in a row are all records.

Margins. City often won by playing a style nobody could copy: controlling games so completely that opponents rarely had chances.

The treble. The 2023 treble, finished with the Champions League final in Istanbul, matched United's 1999.

Pep Guardiola, who led Manchester City to six titles in seven seasons. Photo: Steffen Prößdorf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Our verdict

On peak quality, Guardiola's City are the best team the Premier League has seen. On sustained success, Ferguson's United have no equal: 13 titles is more than twice as many as any other manager. If "dynasty" means lasting power, Ferguson wins. If it means the best team at its height, Guardiola does.

What do you think? Make your case in the comments.

Originally published on FootballHub.

posts.title: Rodri: the anchor that held Guardiola's City together
posts.summary: The goal in Istanbul, the equaliser against Villa, a run of over 70 unbeaten games. Why the quietest player in City's midfield became the one they could least afford to lose.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: Rodri playing for Spain, July 2026. Photo: Bryan Berlin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Ask a casual fan to name the stars of Manchester City's best years and they might list Haaland, De Bruyne and Foden. Ask the players and coaches who faced them, and many would start with Rodri.

What a number 6 does at City

In Guardiola's system the deepest midfielder is the hinge of the whole team. With the ball, he sets the tempo: when to circulate patiently, when to play forward. Without it, he is the first line of defence against the counter-attack, the player who stops trouble before it reaches the centre-backs.

Rodri arrived from Atlético Madrid in 2019 to replace Fernandinho, which is a hard act to follow. By the start of the four-in-a-row run he had grown into the role, and by the end he had redefined it.

Doing the simple things, constantly

Rodri's game is built on things that rarely make highlight reels:

  • Positioning. He is almost always in the right place to receive the ball and to protect the space behind it.
  • Tempo. His passing keeps City's possession moving, so opponents never get a moment to reset.
  • Recovery. When City lose the ball, he is usually the one who wins it back or slows the attack down.

He also kept adding to his game. As his confidence grew, he began scoring regularly from distance and arriving late in the box.

The Atatürk Olympic Stadium in Istanbul, venue of the 2023 Champions League final. Photo: Валерий Дед, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

The big moments

For a player valued for consistency, Rodri has a habit of turning up in the biggest games:

  • 22 May 2022, against Aston Villa. City trailed 2-0 on the final day with the title slipping away. Rodri drilled in the equaliser from the edge of the box in a five-minute burst of three goals that won the league.
  • 10 June 2023, the Champions League final. With Inter holding firm in Istanbul, Rodri met a cut-back from Bernardo Silva in the 68th minute and side-footed it into the corner. It was the only goal of the game and it completed City's treble. He was named player of the match.

What happened when he was missing

The strongest argument for Rodri's importance came when he was absent. In autumn 2023 he was sent off against Nottingham Forest and suspended. City lost to Wolves and Arsenal in the league and were knocked out of the League Cup by Newcastle without him. With him in the team, defeats were rare.

That pattern turned into a remarkable run: Rodri went more than 70 matches for club and country without losing. It ended in the 2024 FA Cup final, which City lost to Manchester United. By then he had helped City to a fourth straight league title, and that summer he won the European Championship with Spain. In October 2024 he won the Ballon d'Or, a rare award for a holding midfielder.

The anchor

Four in a row was a story of change. Strikers, wingers and full-backs came and went. Rodri was the fixed point. Every new idea Guardiola tried, from false nines to the John Stones 3-2 box, was built on the assumption that Rodri would be in the middle, keeping the shape and the ball. For City, the clearest sign of his value was how ordinary they looked without him.

Originally published on FootballHub.

posts.title: John Stones, the centre-back who won City the Champions League from midfield
posts.summary: In the spring of 2023 Guardiola found the last piece of his treble team, and it was a defender. How Stones stepping into midfield built the 3-2 shape that beat Real Madrid and Inter.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: John Stones playing for England, June 2026. Photo: Bryan Berlin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

For most of 2022-23, Manchester City were very good. From around March, they were close to unplayable. The change wasn't a signing or a new striker. It was John Stones taking a few steps forward.

The problem Guardiola had to solve

Guardiola's teams want five players in a strong position behind the ball when they attack, so that if possession is lost the counter-attack is stopped before it starts. For years City built that structure with full-backs who moved into midfield, such as João Cancelo.

By early 2023 that option was gone. Cancelo had left on loan, and Guardiola wanted defenders who were strong one against one. His solution was to start with four natural centre-backs and make one of them a midfielder whenever City had the ball.

Pep Guardiola at RB Leipzig v Manchester City in the Champions League, October 2023. Photo: Steffen Prößdorf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

The 3-2 box

Out of possession, City defended with a back four. With the ball, Stones stepped out of the defensive line and alongside Rodri. The shape became:

  • Three at the back: typically Manuel Akanji, Rúben Dias and Nathan Aké, spread across the pitch.
  • Two in front of them: Rodri and Stones, side by side.
  • Five ahead: Kevin De Bruyne and İlkay Gündoğan between the lines, Bernardo Silva and Jack Grealish wide, Erling Haaland through the middle.

That 3-2 base gave City two layers of protection. If an opponent won the ball, there were five players already positioned to stop the counter. And because Stones was a centre-back by trade, the moment City lost possession he could drop straight back into the defensive line.

Why Stones

Plenty of defenders can pass. Very few can receive the ball in midfield with an opponent behind them, turn, and play forward. Stones had been doing a version of this for years, carrying the ball out of defence. In the new role he became a genuine extra midfielder: he broke lines with passes, rotated with Rodri, and sometimes pushed further forward to support the attack.

The results came quickly. City beat Liverpool 4-1 and Arsenal 4-1 at the Etihad in April 2023, controlling both games. In the Champions League semi-final second leg, they beat Real Madrid 4-0, perhaps the most complete performance of the Guardiola era.

The Atatürk Olympic Stadium in Istanbul, venue of the 2023 Champions League final. Photo: Валерий Дед, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Istanbul

The final against Inter on 10 June 2023 was tense and far less fluent. Inter defended deep and narrow, De Bruyne went off injured in the first half, and City's chances were rare. Stones's role there was less about creating than controlling: keeping the ball moving, giving Rodri a passing option and making sure Inter's forwards had no easy route through the middle.

The game was settled in the 68th minute when Rodri swept in the only goal. City held on for a 1-0 win, their first Champions League title, completing the treble.

The legacy of the role

The "centre-back into midfield" idea has since spread across Europe, but in 2023 it was new enough to catch opponents out. Stones made it work because he combined two skill sets that normally belong to different players. For one spring, City effectively had an extra midfielder without losing a defender, and they won every trophy available.

Originally published on FootballHub.

posts.title: Kevin De Bruyne and the right half-space: the engine of four in a row
posts.summary: Haaland scored the goals and Rodri held the shape, but the chances usually started with De Bruyne drifting into the gap between full-back and centre-back. Here's how City worked with him and without him.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: Kevin De Bruyne playing for Belgium, March 2026. Photo: Bryan Berlin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

Every great team has a player who decides where the danger comes from. For most of Manchester City's four straight titles, that player was Kevin De Bruyne, and the danger came from one area of the pitch: the right half-space.

The zone

The half-space is the channel between the touchline and the middle, the gap between an opposing full-back and his nearest centre-back. Defenders hate it, because nobody is sure whose job it is to step out.

De Bruyne lived there. Starting from a right-sided midfield role, he would drift wide of the opposing midfield and receive the ball facing forward. From that position he had three options, and defenders had to guess which:

  • The cross behind the line. His speciality: a whipped, low ball curling between the goalkeeper and the defenders, onto the run of a striker or the far-side winger.
  • The through ball. If the full-back stepped up to close him down, the space behind opened for a runner.
  • The shot. Leave him alone at the edge of the box and he could finish with either foot.

Why it mattered so much

City's style relies on patience. They keep the ball and wait for an opening. The risk is that a well-organised defence never offers one. De Bruyne was the player who did not need an opening. He could create a chance from a position that looked safe to defend, and that changed how deep defences could sit.

He was the league's Player of the Season in 2021-22, scoring 15 league goals, his best tally, as City edged out Liverpool. In 2022-23 he led the league in assists again, many of them for Erling Haaland, and the two formed the most productive partnership in the division.

Phil Foden at RB Leipzig v Manchester City in the Champions League, October 2023. Photo: Steffen Prößdorf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

2023-24: life without him

The fourth title is the one that shows how much City had built around him, and how much they had built beyond him. De Bruyne injured his hamstring in the opening game at Burnley in August 2023 and needed surgery. He did not return until January.

City adjusted rather than replaced him:

  • Phil Foden moved inside. Used more centrally and in the right half-space himself, Foden had the best season of his career and was named Player of the Season.
  • Bernardo Silva carried more of the build-up, linking midfield to attack with shorter passes rather than De Bruyne's long, early balls.
  • Julián Álvarez offered movement between the lines, pulling defenders out of position for others.

City did not look quite as dangerous, but they stayed in the race. Then De Bruyne came back, at Newcastle in January, off the bench with City trailing 2-1. He equalised, then set up Oscar Bobb's late winner in a 3-2 victory. It was a reminder of what the team had been missing.

The lasting picture

De Bruyne's time at City brought six league titles and the 2023 Champions League, although an injury forced him off in the first half of that final in Istanbul. Much of the four-in-a-row story belongs to Guardiola's system and the players who kept it running. But when people picture City carving a defence open in those years, the image is usually the same: De Bruyne in the right half-space, head up, about to bend the ball into a gap nobody else saw.

Originally published on FootballHub.

posts.title: Four in a row: how Guardiola's City rewrote English football history
posts.summary: From 2020-21 to 2023-24, Manchester City won four straight league titles, something no team had ever done in the English top flight. Each one was won a different way.
posts.bodyHtml:
Cover photo: The City of Manchester Stadium, Manchester City's home. Photo: Arne Müseler, cropped by Blackcat, CC BY-SA 3.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

For more than a century, three titles in a row was the ceiling in English football. Huddersfield Town managed it in the 1920s, Arsenal in the 1930s, Liverpool in the 1980s and Manchester United twice under Sir Alex Ferguson. Nobody had ever won four.

Between 2020-21 and 2023-24, Pep Guardiola's Manchester City did. What stands out is not only the streak but how different each title was. City did not repeat one formula four times. They kept rebuilding the team while they were winning with it.

2020-21: the reset

The season started badly. City were mid-table in December, the attack looked slow, and the squad had no recognised striker in form. Guardiola's answer was to play without one. Bernardo Silva, Phil Foden, İlkay Gündoğan and Kevin De Bruyne rotated through the middle, and Gündoğan became the team's top scorer from midfield.

At the back, the arrival of Rúben Dias changed everything. Paired with a resurgent John Stones, he gave City a defensive line that could hold a high position without panicking. A long winning run through the winter turned a chase into a procession, and City finished the season as clear champions.

2021-22: the final-day comeback

This was the closest of the four, a season-long duel with Jürgen Klopp's Liverpool. It came down to the last afternoon at the Etihad, where City trailed Aston Villa 2-0 with about a quarter of an hour left.

Then, in roughly five minutes, Gündoğan scored, Rodri equalised and Gündoğan scored again. City won 3-2 and finished one point ahead of Liverpool. It remains one of the most dramatic finishes the league has seen, and it showed the squad's depth: the goals came from a substitute and a holding midfielder.

2022-23: Haaland and the treble

Erling Haaland arrived and broke the Premier League scoring record for a single season with 36 goals. City spent much of the year behind Mikel Arteta's Arsenal, but the spring changed the shape of the title race. Guardiola moved John Stones from centre-back into midfield when City had the ball, building a 3-2 base that made them almost impossible to counter.

City overtook Arsenal and won the league, then the FA Cup against Manchester United, then the Champions League against Inter in Istanbul. It was only the second treble in English men's football.

Phil Foden at RB Leipzig v Manchester City in the Champions League, October 2023. Photo: Steffen Prößdorf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

2023-24: four

The fourth title had to be won without the player who had defined much of the era. Kevin De Bruyne was injured in the opening game at Burnley and missed most of the first half of the season. Phil Foden stepped into the space, playing more centrally than before, and was named the league's Player of the Season.

Arsenal pushed City all the way again. City went unbeaten in the league from early December, kept winning through the run-in and beat West Ham on the final day to finish two points clear. Four in a row was done.

Pep Guardiola at RB Leipzig v Manchester City in the Champions League, October 2023. Photo: Steffen Prößdorf, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (source)

What made it possible

Three things stand out across the four seasons:

  • Constant renewal. Players such as Sergio Agüero, Fernandinho, Raheem Sterling and Riyad Mahrez left during the run. City sold or released stars while they were still winning and replaced them before the decline showed.
  • Control first. Whatever the formation, City dominated the ball, and the fewer chances opponents had, the fewer points City dropped.
  • A spine that never moved. Ederson, Dias, Rodri and De Bruyne sat at the centre of almost every season, giving Guardiola fixed points while he changed everything around them.

Four in a row will be the benchmark for every dominant team that follows. The interesting question is not whether someone will match it, but whether anyone will do it while changing as much as City did along the way.

posts.title: Inverted full-backs: why the wide defender keeps drifting inside
posts.summary: The full-back who steps into midfield isn't a gimmick. It is a fix for the oldest problem in possession football: how to stay compact after you lose the ball.
posts.bodyHtml:
Watch a possession-heavy side build from the back and you will often see a full-back do something odd. Instead of hugging the touchline, he walks infield and stands next to the holding midfielder.

The problem it solves

A team that keeps the ball high up the pitch is always one misplaced pass away from a counter-attack. Traditional full-backs bomb forward, so when possession is lost the centre of the pitch is wide open.

Moving a full-back inside creates a 2-3 or 3-2 shape behind the ball:

  • two or three defenders who never leave their zone,
  • two midfielders screening the most dangerous passing lanes,
  • wingers and forwards free to stay high and wide.

What it costs

Width has to come from somewhere else. The winger must stay glued to the line, which suits some players and wastes others. The inverted full-back also needs a midfielder's skills: receiving on the half-turn, scanning before the ball arrives, and passing under pressure.

What to watch for

Next time you see the tactic, track the full-back in the seconds after possession is lost. If he is already in the central lane, the counter-press starts with five players around the ball rather than three. That is the real point of the move.

Originally published by FootballHub Editorial on FootballHub.

posts.title: Set pieces are the most honest edge in football
posts.summary: Corners and free kicks can be rehearsed in a way open play never can. That is why more clubs now treat them as a specialist discipline.
posts.bodyHtml:
Open play is chaos. Set pieces are the only moments in a match when a coach can script almost everything: the starting positions, the decoy runs, the blocks and the delivery.

Why the edge is real

A typical team gets plenty of corners and wide free kicks in a match. If rehearsed routines turn even a small share of those into goals, that adds up over a 38-game season, and it can be the gap between mid-table and Europe.

The building blocks

  • Delivery zones. In-swinging balls aimed at the six-yard box force the goalkeeper to decide. Out-swingers give attackers a run at the ball.
  • Screens. Legal blocks that stop a marker following his man are the modern equivalent of a basketball pick.
  • The second ball. Many set-piece goals come from the clearance, not the first header. Good teams station players to recycle it.

Defending them

Zonal, man-to-man or a hybrid: none is universally best. What matters is that every player knows his job, and that the team practises the specific threats of its next opponent.

The beauty of set pieces is that they reward preparation over talent. For a club without the budget to buy elite forwards, that is the most honest edge in the game.

Originally published by FootballHub Editorial on FootballHub.

posts.title: Reading a high press: triggers, traps and cover shadows
posts.summary: A good press isn't eleven players running at the ball. It's a shared set of cues that tells everyone when to jump and where to herd the opponent.
posts.bodyHtml:
Pressing looks like energy. Underneath, it is information. Every player needs to know the same answer to one question: when do we go?

Common pressing triggers

  1. A pass back to the goalkeeper.
  2. A centre-back receiving on his weaker foot.
  3. A sideways pass into a full-back near the touchline.
  4. A poor first touch.

Each trigger signals that the receiver's options just shrank, and that is the moment to close him down.

Cover shadows

The first presser rarely aims straight at the ball. He curves his run so his body blocks a passing lane behind him. That "shadow" removes an option without anyone needing to mark it.

Traps

The best presses deliberately leave one pass open, usually out to the touchline, and then collapse on it. The touchline acts as an extra defender.

When it fails

If one player jumps late, a gap opens between the lines, and a single pass breaks the whole structure. That is why pressing teams train the press as a unit, and why fatigue late in games is so costly for them.

Originally published by FootballHub Editorial on FootballHub.

posts.title: The quiet return of the back three
posts.summary: Three centre-backs used to signal caution. Used well, the shape now gives attacking teams more width and more security at the same time.
posts.bodyHtml:
For a while the back four seemed to have won. Now three-centre-back systems are back across the league, often in disguise.

Why three at the back again

  • Width without risk. Wing-backs can push high because a third centre-back covers the space behind them.
  • Build-up numbers. Three players across the back make it hard for two strikers to press effectively.
  • Flexibility. Many teams build with three and defend with four, or the other way round, depending on the phase of play.

The 3-4-2-1 in particular

Two narrow attacking midfielders behind a striker occupy the spaces between the opponent's full-backs and centre-backs. Defenders are forced to choose who steps out, and the choice is usually wrong for someone.

The weaknesses

The space outside the wide centre-backs is the classic target. A quick winger isolated there, with the wing-back caught upfield, is the scenario every three-at-the-back coach fears.

Formations are only starting positions, but this one has earned its comeback.

posts.title: Expected goals without the jargon
posts.summary: xG is just a way of asking how good a chance was. Here is how to use it without pretending it predicts the future.
posts.bodyHtml:
Expected goals (xG) puts a number on a simple idea: some chances are better than others.

How it works

Models look at thousands of past shots with similar features: distance, angle, type of assist, header or foot, and whether the shooter was under pressure. If shots like this one went in 12% of the time, it is worth 0.12 xG.

What it is good for

  • Judging whether a team creates good chances or just lots of shots.
  • Spotting finishing streaks that are unlikely to last.
  • Comparing defences by the quality of chances they allow, not just goals conceded.

What it is not

xG does not know about the striker's form, the goalkeeper's positioning in most models, or a deflection that changed everything. A single match's xG is noisy. Over a season it becomes far more meaningful.

A healthy way to use it

Treat xG as a question, not an answer. When a team keeps beating its xG, ask why: elite finishers, or luck that will even out? Either answer is interesting.

Originally published by FootballHub Editorial on FootballHub.

posts.title: Why the No. 6 is the hardest position to scout
posts.summary: The holding midfielder's best work happens off the ball and away from the camera. Highlight reels barely show it.
posts.bodyHtml:
Scouts can measure a winger's dribbles and a striker's shots. The defensive midfielder's most important contributions are often things that didn't happen.

The invisible work

  • Standing in the passing lane so the opponent never tries the pass.
  • Moving five metres to cover a full-back who has pushed on.
  • Receiving under pressure and playing the simple ball that relieves it.

None of that shows up in a goals-and-assists column.

What to look for instead

  1. Scanning. Count how often the player checks over his shoulder before receiving.
  2. Body shape. Does he receive side-on, ready to play forward?
  3. Positional discipline. Where is he when his team loses the ball?

Why it matters

Many title-winning sides have been built around a No. 6 who rarely made headlines. When that player is missing, the whole structure feels looser, even if nobody can quite say why.

Originally published by FootballHub Editorial on FootballHub.

posts.title: What newly promoted sides can learn from the first ten games
posts.summary: The jump to the top flight is mostly about margins. The first ten matches decide how much pressure the rest of the season brings.
posts.bodyHtml:
Promotion brings a step up in speed, precision and punishment for mistakes. The clubs that settle quickest tend to share a few habits.

Pick an identity and keep it

Abandoning the style that won promotion at the first defeat rarely works. Small adjustments to defensive depth and pressing height usually beat a full rebuild.

Defend the box first

Top-flight forwards punish loose marking far more often. Compact defending around the penalty area keeps games close, and close games give a promoted side a chance.

Win the transitions

Many goals for promoted teams come from fast breaks after winning the ball. Having two quick outlets ready changes how opponents commit players forward.

Manage the calendar

Fixture lists often look harder than they are. Treat the first ten games as a block and judge progress on performances, not single results.

None of this guarantees survival, but it gives a newly promoted squad the best chance to stay competitive.

Originally published by FootballHub Editorial on FootballHub.
